#9202. Sophia Huitema "Prussian Blue" @ Harper’s Apartment

Harper’s is pleased to announce Prussian Blue, New York–based artist Sophia Huitema’s first solo exhibition with the gallery. The presentation features new works by Huitema and will be on view through April 25, 2026.

Across the seven oil paintings on view, the visual and chemical properties of the pigment Prussian Blue function as a metaphorical anchor, tying together a cast of watchful female figures within Huitema’s hazy, dreamlike worlds. Working within a restrained range of blue and green tones, the paintings evoke a moody atmosphere through cool harmonies and dimly lit interiors. Prussian Blue, derived from chemical processes historically linked to cyanide while also used as an antidote to certain forms of poisoning, embodies a rare duality in which toxicity and protection converge, mirroring the emotionally guarded, ambiguous presence of Huitema’s figures.

The tension between beauty and menace permeates Huitema’s subjects. Elongated figures with exaggerated limbs and slender necks slink through each scene, often directly confronting the viewer’s gaze. Set within opulent surroundings that recall Gatsby–era decadence, Huitema’s women bear the markers of high society themselves, dressed in elegant gowns and adorned with pearl necklaces or jewel-studded headdresses. Moving through film-noir settings with poise and a quietly calculating air, these femme fatales seem either to lure their audience into a seductive ruse or to deploy their own cunning to evade danger. In Sleeper Car, for example, a woman fitted in a backless evening gown tilts her head slyly over her right shoulder in a relaxed pose while her right hand appears braced and ready to strike. As rain streaks across the coach’s windows and the narrow aisle stretches into an uncertain depth, a moment of cinematic suspense emerges, evoking the apex of a psychological thriller. In this way, Huitema constructs a world of heightened atmosphere and theatrical tension that opens onto the broader visual traditions and painterly languages informing her work.

Huitema’s paintings draw on a range of art-historical and visual references while maintaining a distinct internal coherence. The attenuated proportions and stylized poses of her figures recall traditions of early twentieth-century fashion illustration and Art Deco design, where gesture and embellishment echo the streamlined finesse of illustrators such as Erté and the theatrical poise found in interwar couture and stage design. Her compressed spaces also suggest affinities with aspects of Symbolist and Surrealist painting, in which shallow interiors and phantasmagoric backdrops function less as coherent environments than as psychological realms shaped by subconscious experience. Rather than aligning with a single historical framework, Huitema synthesizes these influences into a contemporary visual language that moves fluidly between illustration, painting, and cinematic staging. Working outside formal academic training, she has developed this vocabulary through sustained studio practice and close observation, resulting in a body of work that situates itself in dialogue with art history while remaining grounded in a self-directed approach to image making. In this context, Prussian Blue operates not only as a chromatic throughline but also as a conceptual one, binding together Huitema’s historical references and recurring motifs of protection and threat in constant tension.

#9201. Venice exhibition tells the story of the man who brought together contemporary artists and Murano’s master glassblowers

Jean Cocteau with the glass master Ermanno Nason in Murano, around 1957 © Archivio Fucina degli Angeli, Venezia, by SIAE 2026

In 1952, Egidio Costantini, an entrepreneur based in Venice, had a brainwave: to take the designs of contemporary artists and, with the collaboration of master glassblowers on the island of Murano, to make artistic sculptures in glass. This was a different approach from that adopted by traditional furnaces like Venini in their decorative glassware, which, although it increasingly involved international designers, was often produced in large, commercially dictated series.

Three years later, Costantini established the Fucina degli Angeli gallery to exhibit the results of his experiment. From then until the 1970s, when other glassmaking companies began to compete, Costantini played a pioneering role in the evolution of glass in Venice, acting as interpreter for more than 100 international artists to Murano’s master glassblowers.

An exhibition opening at the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice this month, curated by the art historian Cristina Beltrami, will tell the Fucina’s story from the 1950s to the 1980s. It will also examine the little-documented but vital role played behind the scenes by Peggy Guggenheim herself, whose purchase of many items helped sustain the gallery financially and whose connections enabled Costantini to exhibit his glass across Europe and even in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. (As it happens, the collector is also the focus of an exhibition opening this month at the Royal Academy of Arts in London, about her Mayfair gallery of the late 1930s—Peggy Guggenheim in London: The Making of a Collector, 21 November-14 March 2027.)

More than 100 works, including glass, painting and sculpture, will be on display in Venice, as well as material from the Fucina’s archives, which have never before been studied in depth. These will be exhibited in 11 rooms organised by artist and theme, and will include glass translations of works by many luminaries of the period, from Max Ernst and Oskar Kokoschka to Lucio Fontana and Paul Jenkins.

Peggy Guggenheim among her glass artworks and guests at Palazzo Venier dei Leoni, Venice, in 1964 © Getty Images, by SIAE 2026

Born in Brindisi in the south of Italy in 1912, Costantini established himself permanently in Venice, where he had been raised and educated, at the beginning of the 1950s. There he became a commercial agent for several of Murano’s glassworks. It was the time of Italy’s post-war economic boom and the city was teeming with creative energy. Costantini seems to have found no difficulty in assembling a group of Venetian artists to form the Study Centre for Painters in the Art of Glass, a collective that exhibited its work at the furnace of Ferro & Lazzarini in 1953.

The next step was to involve international artists of even greater stature. Acting on his own initiative, Costantini had glass versions made of some ceramic sculptures by Pablo Picasso and then travelled to Picasso’s house in Vallauris, near Cannes, to show him the results. In return, Picasso gave Costantini a copy of the book Faunes et Nymphes de Pablo Picasso (1952). This survives in the archives with markings on the images of ceramic figures that were later reinterpreted as glass sculptures at the Fucina. But who made the markings remains a mystery.

The name “Fucina degli Angeli” (smithy of the angels) was proposed by the French writer and artist Jean Cocteau, a long-term friend and collaborator, apparently in reference to Costantini’s large family. The Austrian Expressionist artist Kokoschka contributed an emblematic sketch of two angels holding up an anvil, which he dedicated to the gallery and its founder, “who first succeeded in making me fascinated with the glass of Murano”.

Max Ernst’s King (Re) and Queen (Regina), both from 1964 © Max Ernst, by SIAE 2026

Cocteau enjoyed designing extravagant mythological heads for the Fucina, as well as visiting the furnaces and discussing his ideas with the maestri. Both he and Jean Arp, the German sculptor and painter whose work also features in the exhibition, were “seduced by the colour” of glass and its richness, Beltrami says.

The results, though, may not have pleased everyone. The Swiss artist Walter Bodmer allowed his sketch Asymmetric Cat (1955) to be transformed into an oversimplified glass vessel. But after this, for reasons unknown, he never participated again.

The exhibition looks set to offer a fascinating insight into a very personal approach to collaborations between artist and craftsman, as well as an evocative record of an under-appreciated chapter in Venetian history.

• Fucina degli Angeli: Peggy Guggenheim and 20th-Century Artistic Glass, Peggy Guggenheim Collection, Venice, 14 November-29 March 2027

The money will be divided between improvements to the original Peggy Guggenheim Collection and a feasibility study for the Foundation’s expansion

The Venice Glass Week is a city-wide collaboration between museums, commercial galleries and artisans of Murano

An upcoming exhibition explores the brief but intense creative spark that lay the foundations for Italian art of the 1960s

#9200. Photographer Files $150K Copyright Lawsuit Against Sony Over His Image of Stevie Wonder

Photographer Files $150K Copyright Lawsuit Against Sony Over His Image of Stevie Wonder

A photographer has sued Sony, accusing the company of posting his “iconic” 1974 portrait of Stevie Wonder on Instagram without permission.

Longtime photographer Al Satterwhite filed a copyright infringement lawsuit against Sony Music Publishing (SMP) in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York on Sunday, seeking up to $150,000 in damages.

According to a report by Billboard, Satterwhite photographed Wonder sitting at a piano in 1974 and later registered the images with the U.S. Copyright Office. In 2023, SMP allegedly used one of the portraits in an Instagram carousel marking the 50th anniversary of Wonder’s 1973 album Innervisions.

Satterwhite’s lawsuit alleges that SMP posted his “iconic photograph” of Wonder on Instagram without first obtaining a license. He argues that the company’s use of the image cost him a licensing opportunity and potentially affected the market for his work. The complaint also claims that SMP benefited from sharing the photograph with its social media audience without paying him.

In court documents, the photographer claims the alleged infringement by SMP “has harmed, and continues to harm, the potential market for or value of the copyrighted work by robbing Plaintiff of his exclusive right to license the copyrighted work for illustrative and other purposes.”

The photographer is seeking up to $150,000 in statutory damages for copyright infringement, the maximum amount allowed under federal law for the willful infringement of a single work. Satterwhite’s argues that Sony knew, or should have known, that it needed a license to use the image, given its experience handling intellectual property rights in the music industry.

In the complaint, Satterwhite argues that SMP “is a sophisticated media company that understands copyright law and the need to obtain a license to publish the copyrighted works of others.”

According to Billboard, Satterwhite has filed more than a dozen previous lawsuits over the alleged unauthorized use of his photographs of Wonder and other well-known figures, including Arnold Schwarzenegger and Mel Brooks. Satterwhite also filed a lawsuit against Berklee College of Music last year, accusing the institution of using another photograph of Wonder from the same 1974 shoot without permission. He dropped the case voluntarily less than two months later.

#9198. Blackmagic’s $1,695 Spatial Audio Mic Has 108 Mics and Looks Super Sci-Fi

Blackmagic’s $1,695 Spatial Audio Mic Has 108 Mics and Looks Super Sci-Fi

Blackmagic Design has announced the Ambisonic Microphone, a new professional mic designed to capture spatial audio for immersive video productions.

“The Blackmagic Ambisonic Microphone is a 7th order ambisonic microphone array featuring 108 digital MEMS microphones that capture the entire sound field,” Blackmagic explains. “The MEMS microphones are mounted flush in a solid, faceted metal body, making the design extremely strong for professional use while remaining small enough to fit in the palm of your hand, and be mounted on top of a camera.”

Advanced audio processing technology is built directly into the microphone, and an internal processor runs Apple’s encoding filters, converting the 108 MEMS microphones to seventh-order ambisonics in real time. This means customers don’t need complicated software or a breakout box.

The mic is powered by a single USB-C cable, and it can quickly be mounted to an URSA Cine Immersive camera. Capturing spatial audio is as simple as plugging it in.

As Blackmagic Design explains, its new microphone started development when it was working with Apple on the Blackmagic URSA Cine Immersive camera, which was formally announced in June 2024 and billed as “the ultimate camera system for making immersive video for the Apple Vision Pro.”

Filmmakers have used the Blackmagic URSA Cine Immersive to capture all sorts of incredible things, including basketball games and rocket launches.

“This microphone started when we were collaborating with Apple on the Blackmagic URSA Cine Immersive camera. I heard a high resolution spatial audio capture for the first time and it was like hearing an acoustic reality, I was totally blown away,” says Blackmagic Design CEO Grant Petty.

“Apple licensed their array geometry and the ambisonic encoding filters, we did the engineering and design, and the result is an ambisonic microphone where you just plug in one cable and capture true spatial audio.”

The Blackmagic Ambisonic Microphone will be available next month for $1,695 through Blackmagic Design and its authorized retailers.

#9196. Leica Is Giving the M-A and M11-P Hammertone Special Edition Variants

Leica Is Giving the M-A and M11-P Hammertone Special Edition Variants

Leica has announced a new special edition version of both the M-A and M11-P cameras that brings what the company describes as a classic design that it also rarely uses: hammertone.

“Since the 1930s, the hammertone finish has symbolized the combination of durability and technical aesthetics. This distinctive texture is formed during the drying process when metal pigments and special additives create subtle variations in surface tension. In industrial design, particularly in Germany, this finish has come to symbolize functionality and reliability,” Leica says.

While it might be somewhat common generally in Germany, that’s not the case for Leica cameras – at least modern ones. It has appeared in the past, such as from the Leica MD documentation camera for the Leitz Reprovit system to the exceptionally rare Leica MD (of which only ten were produced in 1964), but it’s certainly unusual.

“With their distinctive finish, both variants draw inspiration from rare Leica special editions, including the 1964 Leica MD Hammertone, the 2003 MP LHSA, the 2011 Leica M9 Hammertone, and the 2016 Leica M-A Vienna Edition. The new Leica M-A Hammertone and the new Leica M11-P Hammertone continue this lineage in their own unique way, thereby adding two exceptional, valuable variants to the Leica M portfolio,” Leica says.

Leica says it has reworked the process of applying the pattern for these special editions to achieve a uniform finish of the texture across the entire camera.

Both the M-A and the M11-P have the hammertone finish on the top plate and base plate. It is made from solid brass with a cross knurling on the control elements and a shiny silver shutter-release plate. The cameras also have a black leatherette covering in a vulcanite style with white engravings.

The Leica M11-P Hammertone also has newly rounded, classically styled edges on the top plate and base plate to go with the hammertone texture, as well as a new version of the screw on the front featuring a silver-chrome finish.

This pattern has the special distinction of making every camera unique due to the way it is applied.

Both the Leica M-A Hammertone and the Leica M11-P Hammertone will be available starting on November 12 from Leica Stores, the Leica Online Store, and authorized dealers. The retail price for the Leica M-A Hammertone is $8,000, while the Leica M11-P Hammertone costs $10,950.

#9195. Molly Bounds "The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins" @ Mrs Gallery, Maspeth, NY

Mrs. is pleased to present The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins, Molly Bounds’ New York debut solo exhibition, on view at the gallery’s 6040 56th Drive location. This exhibition marks the Los Angeles-based artist’s second presentation with the gallery following The Armory Show in September 2025. The show will be on view through May 2, 2026.

Opening on the vernal equinox, a rare moment when the hours of daylight and night are equal, Molly Bounds offers light as the protagonist in her new series of paintings. It is versatile and ever-changing; it both conceals and reveals, and reminds us of the unrelenting forward movement of time. Depicting her subjects both in contemplation and in the midst of candid movement, Bounds continues her investigation into liminal moments where stillness and urgency shape the mood. Much like the transition from winter to spring, these figures appear on the threshold of a transformative shift.

There are also moments of escapism. In both It Sings in Me and Among of Green, Again a figure moves freely amongst rolling green hills, illuminated under the sun. The landscape appears bucolic and perhaps overly so - is this real or imagined? For Bounds this is less important; the ability to build optimism and a belief in renewal and rebirth is paramount. Contrasting with the scenes of pensive interiority, these landscapes communicate urgency, celebration, possibility, and fantasy. After the darkness of winter, spring wins.

#9194. South Korean Photographers Demand Police Investigation After Politician Calls Them ‘Hyenas’ in Chatroom

South Korean Photographers Demand Police Investigation After Politician Calls Them ‘Hyenas’ in Chatroom

A leading South Korean politician is facing fierce backlash from the country’s media after referring to photojournalists as a “pack of hyenas” in an online chatroom — an insult that has prompted a formal police complaint from press photographers.

Representative Choi Min-hee is a South Korean politician and senior member of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK), serving in the country’s National Assembly. She has sparked outrage in South Korea after sharing an image of working press photographers in a group chat and making disparaging comments about the photojournalists.

Last week, Min-hee uploaded photos of photographers covering DPK events to a KakaoTalk group chat room for local party members in Namyangju, a city in South Korea. In the post uploaded to the chat room, which had over 500 participants, Min-hee referred to the photographers in the image as a “pack of hyenas.”

“These are journalists from media outlets with access to the National Assembly,” Min-hee writes in the post, according to numerous South Korean news outlets. “They’re doing this to capture divisive footage somehow.”

Min-hee’s disparaging post about South Korean photographers quickly spread online, sparking an angry backlash from members of the press. Amid the uproar, she held a press conference at the National Assembly on Wednesday and apologized for her remarks. However, the Korean Photographers Association has nonetheless decided to file a police complaint against Min-hee for disparaging photographers as a “pack of hyenas.”

The Korean Photographers Association says the politician’s remarks demean journalists, undermine legitimate press scrutiny of those in power, and cross the line from acceptable criticism into defamatory accusations.

“Condemning legitimate reporting activities as political divisiveness and ridiculing journalists by comparing them to animals is a clear insult to media professionals and an inappropriate act with potential for defamation,” the Korean Photographers Association writes in a statement to Wednesday, according to national news outlet Cho Sun Daily.

“Photographers do not exist to capture scenes that suit politicians’ preferences. They exist to monitor power through the eyes of the public and record history. Criticism of the media is free, but insults and baseless accusations against reporters cannot be justified.”

The association says the photographers pictured in Min-hee’s post have suffered significant emotional distress and humiliation as a result.

“We have finalized the decision to file a complaint with the police to prevent infringement on our members’ rights,” the Korean Photographers Association adds. “Photographers whose faces were exposed in the photos are currently experiencing severe humiliation and self-loathing, struggling to the point of being unable to continue their work.”

#9192. Nat Meade's "Franklin" @ HESSE FLATOW, NYC

HESSE FLATOW is pleased to announce the opening of Franklin, an exhibition of paintings and works on paper by Nat Meade, marking his third solo presentation with the gallery. The show is on view through April 18, 2026.

The emotional arc of life’s struggles and triumphs take shape within Meade’s figurative works, reflecting the artist’s everyday experiences as he navigates being a father, son, partner, and academic. Far from portraits of actual individuals, his protagonists mirror timeless archetypes. At times, we encounter a lone traveler searching for existential validation; at other times, we see through intergenerational dynamics. This allegorical distance via painting provides a realm for Meade to explore personal challenges through absurd, somber, and humorous tropes, while also furnishing a space rife with human nature that bears unequivocal resonance.

Meade’s reflections on his relationship with his father after his recent passing, and subsequent reevaluations of his own role as a parent percolate throughout the works in the exhibition. Vulnerability, pain, and mortality are themes Meade does not shy away from, yet the introduction of younger males in this body of work casts a sense of hope, acceptance, reconciliation, and renewal.

Faced with a pair of dangling legs from a cloud in Poise, we question whether a figure is ascending or descending from the heavens, a suggestion perhaps on the interchangeability of birth and death, be it physical or spiritual. Ghostly specters hover over certain individuals – a metaphor for inherited trauma and release. In the same way that a soul peels away from an expiring body in classic cartoons, we observe a spirit looking back on itself with what might be  happiness or regret. The exhibition’s title Franklin is a subtle nod to the 1974 horror film Texas Chainsaw Massacre, known for its portrayal of a deranged patriarchal family. Meade embraces this inner turmoil of contending with one’s violent and antagonistic impulses as his characters are visibly sublimated or put in their place. A vulture picking away at a corpse recalls the eternal punishment of Prometheus by Zeus, while a bearded figure on his hands and knees echoes William Blake’s portrayal of Nebuchadnezzar, condemned for his lust for power.

In contrast to the adults, Meade’s younger figures appear more harmonious. A young boy charts his own path as he steers a boat with a radiant torch, unclouded by societal and familial pressures. A sense of childlike wonder and adventure beholds an adolescent ankle-deep in a secluded cove, reaching in to touch the sea floor brilliantly covered in starfish, anemones, and mussels. In a related work, we observe two pairs of legs belonging to father and son in the same shallow pool, one tenderly guiding the other. Having in the past shown his figures wrestling with or victims of forces of nature, physically being overtaken by turbulent wind and crashing waves, Meade’s focus on calmer seas signals a turning point. He recognizes the need to acknowledge one’s rocky histories in order to heal and release future generations from similar burdens. Despite what may seem like an insurmountable heaviness, he reminds us of the stubborn resilience of human nature, making progress attainable.

#9190. Revisiting Zeiss ZM Lenses Part 2: Learning to Like the 35mm Lens

Revisiting Zeiss ZM Lenses Part 2: Learning to Like the 35mm Lens

The 35mm focal length is the most popular prime lens on the planet, and for part two of our look at the Zeiss ZM lenses, I’m not just going to talk about one lens; I’m showing you three!

In our previous look at the Zeiss ZM line of lenses, I tested the wider-angle lenses in the ZM lineup. This time, I took the trio of 35mm lenses that are made by Zeiss to beautiful British Columbia. We are going to celebrate photography together, learn about the history and character of the ZM lenses, and I’m going to take you on an adventure across Vancouver Island.

Full disclosureThis story was made possible in partnership with Zeiss. Read part one here.

Now, part of this whole Zeiss showcase is for me to learn about all these famous optical formulas that I heard about as a young photographer but didn’t really understand. I also wanted to make an effort to at least appreciate the 35mm focal length, even if it’s not my usual choice. Using three lenses that have identical framing meant really focusing on the subtle differences, so let’s start with the most general-purpose of the trio.

The Biogon 35mm f/2 was one of the first lenses that Zeiss created back in 2005, and for good reason. The 35mm lens is a staple of rangefinder photography due to its storytelling ability and versatility as a street photo lens. It made sense to start with a lens that would be a good balance of both physical compactness and light-gathering ability, and the Biogon 35mm f/2 was the result.

Zeiss lenses do tend to be slightly larger because optical engineers feel it best to correct for distortion and deliver sharp clarity right to the edge of the frame. I still found the 8.5-ounce (240-gram) lens to be easy to carry without being too obtrusive through the viewfinder.

The lens worked as a great general-purpose optic, and the f/2 aperture with its 10-blade design delivered pleasant bokeh. Even more impressive is the flare control, and I found this very useful when shooting at Butchart Gardens on a very sunny day. I decided to also shoot some 35mm film with the Zeiss Ikon rangefinder camera, and this is where the almost complete lack of distortion really shone. The Biogon f/2 is probably the most practical of the three available options, but I may have had even more fun with the next one.

The Biogon “C” stands for compactness, and Zeiss certainly achieved this goal. The little f/2.8 lens is only 7 ounces (200 grams) and fits so neatly on the front of the camera that I could tuck the Leica M11-P I was using into a jacket pocket. This turned out to be useful because I headed up to Cowichan Bay, and the classic Vancouver Island rain decided to settle in.

For a slight compromise in f-stop, the C version is far handier, and as I explored the marina, I was snapping away at interesting textures and stunning sunsets. Even at dusk, the little lens still gathered enough light, and the clarity was astoundingly good. I also found that the bokeh had a very pleasant look to it, and the usual lack of distortion and flare control returned.

More importantly, though, the compact C lens still had nice controls, and I found it natural to use despite its small size. The 43mm filter threads also came in handy when I used some ND filters to get slow shutter speeds. I ended my time with this little lens shooting landscapes under a charming stone bridge before heading to the capital city of Victoria.

I arrived in Victoria quite late at night, so I decided it was a perfect time to test out the brightest of the Zeiss 35mm lenses. This lens uses a reverse-telephoto design to keep the light striking the film plane as perpendicular as possible while still providing incredible light-gathering potential.

Again, the lens proved, in typical Zeiss fashion, to be extremely sharp and well-corrected. However, the 10-blade aperture and very shallow depth of field wide open really impressed me with beautiful sunstars and soft specular highlights. Bokeh is soft and smooth, and backgrounds just fade off into a gentle blur.

This does come with a compromise in size and weight, with the Distagon formula being easily the largest of the three lenses. It will tip the scales at about 13.4 ounces (380 grams) and takes 49mm filters, so the physical diameter of the lens is significantly more robust. I did see it in the corner of the framelines as well, but this all felt worth it when shooting in such dim conditions. Even wide open at f/1.4, sharpness was excellent, and although I don’t normally go for the fastest glass, I actually prefer brighter apertures with 35mm lenses. I feel like I can separate a subject more easily with a 35mm f/1.4, and the Distagon quickly became my favorite of the three.

I had a wonderful adventure on the island, and it really forced me to get to grips with the versatility of a 35mm lens. I shot everything from portraits and street photography to landscapes and night photography. Having three different options was really enjoyable, allowing me to see the nuances between these otherwise similar optics. Of the three choices, I gravitated toward the slowest and fastest of the lenses because the bokeh seemed the nicest. However, the f/1.4 is a little too big sometimes, and the f/2 would probably be my choice if I were only going to take one. Regardless, I liked them all and never felt like I was at a disadvantage when shooting with them. In fact, it was quite the opposite.

The journey doesn’t end here, though. Keep an eye out for part three of our showcase about Zeiss ZM lenses, where I get to use my favorite 50mm focal length and see what Zeiss has to offer. We have a stunning location to end things, and it’s a place from my childhood that I haven’t returned to in forty years.

Full disclosureThis story was made possible in partnership with Zeiss.

#9188. Chris “Daze” Ellis "Orchid Rain on the Underground" @ PPOW Gallery, NYC

PPOW are pleased to present Orchid Rain on the Underground, Chris “Daze” Ellis’s third solo exhibition with the gallery. The show is on view through April 25, 2026. Featuring a new series of paintings, multimedia installation, and a site-specific mural, the exhibition harnesses the passion and spontaneity of the graffiti movement of the 1970s and 80s while demonstrating a thoughtful and meticulous practice honed over the past five decades. While the version of New York City that fostered Daze’s beginnings as a fine artist may feel like a bygone era, the works in this exhibition are evidence of its enduring legacy. By revitalizing that foundational energy for the present moment, Daze affirms the continued relevance of those figures and places, and their profound influence on the creative spirit that persists throughout the city today.

Born in Brooklyn in 1962, Daze became inspired by early graffiti writers like Blade, Lee Quiñones, and PHASE 2 while attending High School of Art and Design in the mid 1970s. As he began to establish his own name as an artist, he was also a frequent visitor to what would become historic landmarks of the city’s nightlife, including the Lit Lounge in the East Village, Danceteria on West 21st Street, and the Mudd Club in Tribeca. These nightclubs, which often doubled as art galleries and performance venues, functioned as generative sites of social and artistic experimentation and part of the driving force behind Daze’s early works. By the early 1980s, he had begun transitioning from tagging subway cars to developing a studio practice that encapsulates the ethos of the city.

Inspired by early 20th-century urban realist artists, including John Sloan of the Ashcan School and Reginald Marsh of the WPA era, Daze’s works honor New York City’s streets and subways as important sites of his creative evolution. Simultaneously influenced by the lyrical abstraction of works by Joan Mitchell and Willem De Kooning, Daze combines gestural swaths of acrylic and spray paint with detailed renderings of train car interiors, tunnels, and stations. In Gem Spa In the 80s, 2025, Daze depicts the now iconic newspaper stand and candy store that once operated on the corner of St. Mark’s Place and Second Avenue. Gem Spa was a central destination and meeting place for members of the city’s subcultures and is referenced by literary figures like Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg (who called it a “nerve center” of the city). Important people from Daze’s life can be found throughout the composition, among them critic and curator Carlo McCormick as well as artist Martin Wong, who both emerge amongst the crowd in the painting’s foreground. In other works, technicolor throngs of flowers ascend from heaps of urban rubble, representing optimism amidst inequality and the beauty that can arise out of destruction. Throughout the exhibition, these varied combinations of tropical flora and local flowers from the artist’s home in upstate New York function as poignant memorials to what has been lost and hopeful testaments to the beauty and creativity that can still be found around every corner.

The exhibition will also include a site-specific mural, bringing an aspect of Daze’s practice often relegated to the outdoors into the interior setting of the gallery. Covering the walls of a hallway, the mural gives way to the final room of the gallery, featuring a multimedia installation that transports viewers into a composite scene from the artist’s youth. Combining a light-up dance floor and disco ball, actual subway car seats, and a curated track fusing house, disco, hip-hop, and club music, the installation emphasizes the freedom and creative inspiration that arose from these settings, and their importance to Daze’s personal and artistic development. Combining elements from throughout his career, Orchid Rain on the Underground showcases Daze’s never-ending exploration of daily life in New York City while paying homage to the people and places that comprise its vibrant cultural heartbeat.

#9187. Photographer Who Covered High School Football Team for Free for 28 Years Suddenly Banned

Photographer Who Covered High School Football Team for Free for 28 Years Suddenly Banned

A photographer who has covered a Los Angeles high school football team for free over the past 28 years says she was abruptly told she could no longer take photos, despite meeting all the required qualifications.

Photographer Judy Collins has been capturing images of football games at Van Nuys High School — a public high school in the Van Nuys district of Los Angeles that belongs to the Los Angeles Unified School District — for almost three decades. Collins, a grandmother whose two sons graduated from Van Nuys High School, has been providing these images for families free of charge.

However, according to a report by the LA Times, Collins was informed on Friday that she could no longer take photographs at Van Nuys High School despite completing an extension application that complied with Los Angeles Unified School District volunteer policies.

Collins says she had never had issues taking photos at Van Nuys High School until this year. The LA Times reports that football coach Ken Osorio became concerned after noticing that Collins had been told to leave her usual photography position earlier this season. He and the school’s athletic director, Dion Coley, invited her to apply for a volunteer coaching position to address any concerns about her presence on the football sidelines.

Collins paid $80 for a CPR course and another $20 for a tuberculosis screening. She was also fingerprinted and underwent a background check. She had initially been told she would need to pay several hundred dollars for a vendor’s license, despite giving her photographs away for free. The group decided that becoming a volunteer coach would be a quicker way to meet Los Angeles Unified School District requirements.

After completing the paperwork, Collins was told she needed to meet with Martin Tate, the assistant principal in charge of athletics. She says she tried several times to contact him by phone and in person at games but was unable to reach him. However, when Collins arrived at the team’s game on Friday and began taking photographs, Tate confronted her and told her to leave the field.

When Collins asked why, he allegedly told her, “I’m just following the principal’s order.” Collins pointed out that the principal was on administrative leave, but Tate did not change his instruction. The Los Angeles Unified School District’s communication office did not respond to a request for comment from the LA Times.

The news outlet says that Collins has since completed her volunteer coach application and begun photographing games for Panorama High while awaiting permission to return to Van Nuys. She has also obtained the official stamp required to complete her tuberculosis screening, which should allow her to become an officially registered volunteer coach.

#9186. Art Basel offers compensation to dealers after early closure of Paris fair

Art Basel Paris 2026 was shut early due to protests in the French capital

Art Basel will compensate dealers for the early closure of its Paris fair, held from 20-23 October in the Grand Palais, the fair company announced today (11th November), on a French national holiday.

The fair was forced to shut down its Parisian outing two days early because of violent rioting in the French capital. Since then, dealers have been demanding compensation for their lost sales and stand fees. Indeed, soon after the closure the French Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA) sent a strongly worded letter to the fair director, Karim Crippa. It accused the firm of not consulting with dealers—the CPGA represents 57 of the fair’s 211 exhibitors—and of showing “disrespect, even contempt” for them.

The closure hit the smaller dealers particularly hard, since the biggest galleries tended to make sales on the opening days, whereas the smaller dealers, mainly sited on the upper floor of the Grand Palais, depended on the two weekend days for business. The letter said it expected “concrete proposals” for this compensation.

Crippa has responded to the letter with an offer of a reduction across the board of 20% of stand fees to all participants. He said: “We believe this approach offers a fair and considered way forward, reflecting our appreciation of the partnership we share and our commitment to strengthening it further.”

Philippe Charpentier of Mor Charpentier gallery, who is the president of the CPGA, tells The Art Newspaper that the compensation rate is what the committee expected.

Nonetheless, if one calculates in percentages, the fair was open for three-and-a-half days—its ultra-VIP Avant-Première timeslot began at 3pm on Tuesday 20 October, and the fair closed on Friday—instead of the projected five-and-a-half. The fair was therefore shortened by about 36%.

Speaking about the decision to close the fair early, Noah Horowitz, the chief executive of Art Basel, tells The Art Newspaper: “We stand by the decision to close. We feel it was in the right interest of all the parties involved. It was a very difficult decision, but we stand by it.”

Asked about the decision to close for the two days—when unrest was only expected on the Saturday—he says: “Given the uncertainty surrounding the impact and the duration of the planned demonstrations and access to the Grand Palais, we simply couldn't be confident that conditions would allow us to reopen safely on Sunday. An event of this size and scale is incredibly complex, and some exhibitors had also expressed serious concerns about leaving artworks unattended in the Grand Palais on the weekend. We concluded that closing the fair early was in the best interests of the art, the staff and ultimately the visitors.”

Horowitz is not prepared to comment on other aspects of the closure—for example, questions of insurance or the firm’s relationship with the Grand Palais, for which MCH paid €10.6m to rent the space for seven years in 2022. Horowitz says that MCH, the parent company of the Basel group of art fairs, is "fully committed to delivering the 2027 edition of the fair".

The gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

Here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

The gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

The annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

This limit applies per giver, per recipient. That means:

The IRS adjusts this amount for inflation periodically. Here's how the annual exclusion has changed over the years:

The annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

This is the single most important gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. Gifts received are not taxable income.

When you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — currently $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

Let's put that in perspective. If you give your daughter $118,000 in one year, you're $100,000 over the annual exclusion. You file Form 709 to report it, and the IRS subtracts that $100,000 from your lifetime exemption. Your remaining exemption drops from $13.61 million to $13.51 million. No tax is owed.

At the 40% top gift tax rate, you'd need to give away more than $13.61 million over your lifetime before any actual tax kicks in. That puts fewer than 0.1% of Americans in gift tax territory.

Important sunset warning: The current $13.61 million exemption is set to be cut roughly in half on January 1, 2026, reverting to approximately $7 million per person (adjusted for inflation) under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act sunset provisions. This has created urgency for high-net-worth families to make large gifts before the window closes.

Several types of transfers are completely excluded from gift tax rules — no annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required:

The education and medical exclusions are especially powerful for the FI community. A grandparent can pay $50,000 in tuition directly to a university AND give the grandchild $18,000 in cash in the same year — all tax-free with no reporting.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single recipient in a year, you must file IRS Form 709 (United States Gift and Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax Return) with your tax return. Filing Form 709 does not mean you owe tax — it simply reports the gift and tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

One of the most powerful gift tax strategies available is the 529 plan 5-year election. The IRS allows you to front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts into a 529 education savings plan in a single year.

For 2026, that means you can contribute up to $90,000 (5 x $18,000) to a 529 plan for a single beneficiary in one year. A married couple electing gift splitting can contribute up to $180,000 per beneficiary.

The catch: if you use the 5-year election and then pass away during the 5-year period, a prorated portion of the gift returns to your taxable estate.

The gift tax and estate tax share the same $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Think of it as one pool of money that covers both gifts during your life and transfers at death.

Every dollar of lifetime exemption you use for gifts during your life reduces the amount available to shelter your estate from tax at death. However, there's a strategic advantage to giving during your lifetime: future appreciation on gifted assets escapes your taxable estate.

Example: You give your daughter stock worth $1 million today. You use $982,000 of lifetime exemption ($1M minus $18K annual exclusion). If that stock grows to $3 million by the time you die, the full $3 million — including $2 million in appreciation — is completely outside your estate. That's $2 million that will never be subject to estate tax.

A practical guide to making gifts without triggering tax.

Pro tip: There is no limit on the number of recipients. You can give $18,000 each to as many people as you want.

Payments made directly to educational institutions or medical providers for someone else are unlimited and completely excluded from gift tax. These do not reduce your annual exclusion or lifetime exemption.

Pro tip: The payment must go directly to the institution — not to the student or patient. Reimbursing someone for tuition they already paid counts as a gift.

Front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts ($90,000 individual, $180,000 married) into a 529 plan in a single year. The full amount starts compounding immediately.

Pro tip: If you die during the 5-year election period, a prorated portion returns to your estate. File Form 709 to report the 5-year election.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single person, file IRS Form 709 with your tax return. The excess reduces your $13.61 million lifetime exemption but no tax is owed until you exceed it.

Pro tip: Filing Form 709 is just paperwork — it does not mean you owe tax. It simply tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

If your estate is approaching the lifetime exemption threshold, work with an estate planning attorney. Strategies like GRATs, family LLCs, and intentionally defective grantor trusts can transfer wealth beyond the basic gift tax rules.

Gifts received are not considered taxable income. However, if the gifted asset later generates income (like dividends or interest), that income is taxable to the recipient.

No annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required. If your spouse is not a US citizen, a higher annual exclusion applies ($185,000 for 2026) instead of the unlimited deduction.

Gifts are not reported on your income tax return (Form 1040). If you gave more than $18,000 to any single recipient, you file a separate Form 709 (gift tax return) alongside your income tax return. The recipient does not report the gift on their income tax return either. Gifts are outside the income tax system entirely.

The gift tax affects far fewer people than most assume. With an $18,000 annual exclusion per recipient, a $13.61 million lifetime exemption, and unlimited exclusions for direct tuition and medical payments, the vast majority of Americans can give generously without ever owing a penny in gift tax. The key rules: the giver pays (not the receiver), gifts are not taxable income, and filing Form 709 is just tracking — not a tax bill. For FI families, strategic gifting is one of the most powerful ways to accelerate the next generation's financial independence while reducing your taxable estate.

#9183. NVIDIA’s Longtime CEO, Jensen Huang, Resigns In Disgrace

NVIDIA’s Longtime CEO, Jensen Huang, Resigns In Disgrace

NVIDIA’s longtime CEO, Jensen Huang, has resigned following multiple affairs, including one with an alleged spy and a second with an executive who reported directly to him.

It has been a whirlwind week for NVIDIA, one of the world’s richest tech companies. Last Sunday, NVIDIA announced it was investigating Huang following reports that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The situation got even worse yesterday when reports of Huang having an affair with one of NVIDIA’s top executives came to light.

NVIDIA says its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO until the company names a permanent successor. The company’s board began its search immediately.

NVIDIA’s board has also appointed director Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair. Jones, an investor and chip design executive, has been on NVIDIA’s board since 1993, when the company was founded in San Jose.

“I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period,” NVIDIA’s new interim CEO wrote in a memo to employees, as reported by The Wall Street Journal.

“We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us,” Kress continued.

For Jensen Huang, this marks a disastrous end to what had otherwise been an incredible run at the helm. Since NVIDIA’s founding, its valuation has increased by more than 400,000%. In just the past five years, during the AI arms race, the company’s stock has surged nearly 430%, making NVIDIA a $4.5 trillion company.

“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones.

“She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption,” Jones continued.

NVIDIA is slated to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results on Tuesday, November 17, as previously scheduled. Its stock has dropped around 15% this week due to Huang’s scandals and is down over 28% in just the last month. Year to date, NVIDIA’s stock has plunged about 16%.

#9181. Photographer Travels the World to Show the Beauty of Bugs

Photographer Travels the World to Show the Beauty of Bugs

Photographer Dara Ojo began his macro journey while living in China during the pandemic. Initially, it was a way to explore the natural world during lockdowns, but it became a bigger obsession for the Nigerian-born photographer.

In the intervening six years, Ojo has photographed insects in China, Costa Rica, Canada, Mexico, and Nigeria.

Ojo has taken all of that work and compiled it into a newly released, 290-page book titled Tiny Titans: The Silent Keepers of Our Ecosystem. He tells PetaPixel about his approach to macro photography.

“I photograph living creatures in their natural environments. I don’t harm, manipulate, or stage my subjects, and I try to document their behavior as naturally as possible,” he explains.

“Patience is probably the most important part of my approach. In macro photography, particularly at high magnifications, the smallest movements can completely change a photograph. A slight breeze, a moving leaf, or an insect turning its head can mean starting all over again.”

Ojo says that to combat this, he will photograph early in the morning when temperatures are cooler and insects are less active, as well as at night, when a different world emerges.

“Technically, I frequently use focus bracketing and stacking to achieve the level of detail I want,” he says. “At extreme magnification, the depth of field is incredibly shallow, so I may need to capture multiple images at different focal points and combine them into a single photograph.”

Ojo takes PetaPixel through some of his favorite and memorable moments from his new book, including the front cover, which has a special meaning for him.

“I photographed it at Lufasi Nature Park in Lagos, Nigeria, where I’m originally from,” Ojo explains. “I remember really enjoying that particular encounter. Praying mantises are wonderful subjects to photograph because of their remarkable appearance, expressive movements and the way they seem to observe you just as closely as you’re observing them. It was one of those genuinely fun photographic experiences.”

“It’s one of those subjects that reminds me why I find the natural world so endlessly fascinating,” Ojo says of the image above. “At first glance, it might appear strange or even unsettling, but there’s an extraordinary biological story behind it.”

“Certain fungi infect arthropods and eventually produce structures that emerge from their bodies, helping the fungus reproduce and spread. It’s a remarkable example of the complex relationships that exist in nature, including those we rarely notice,” he continues.

“Photographing something like this is particularly special because you’re documenting a biological interaction that many people will never encounter firsthand.”

“Spiders are among the most misunderstood creatures I photograph, and I think this image challenges people’s perceptions in a beautiful way,” Ojo says.

“Many people associate spiders with fear, but here is a mother carrying and protecting her young. Female wolf spiders are known for this extraordinary parental behavior, with the spiderlings riding on their mother’s back after emerging from the egg sac.”

“It’s precisely the kind of image I want people to encounter in Tiny Titans. Something that initially inspires fear can suddenly inspire curiosity, admiration, and perhaps even empathy.”

Tiny Titans: The Silent Keepers of Our Ecosystem is published by Rocky Mountain Books and available for $45.

More of Ojo’s work can be seen on his Instagram and website.

#9179. The Director of ‘Knives Out’ Has Just Released a $13 Camera App

The Director of ‘Knives Out’ Has Just Released a $13 Camera App

Director Rian Johnson and cinematographer Steve Yedlin are used to teaming up to make films and TV shows like Looper and Knives Out. But the two recently collaborated on a smaller screen: a camera app for iPhone.

Since Chromagraph Camera was released on the App Store last week, it briefly hit the number one spot on the paid charts.

“So I recently badgered my cinematographer Steve Yedlin into making my ideal iPhone still camera app,” Johnson says on X (formerly Twitter). “It shoots RAW, bypasses the iPhone’s look processing and instead uses the same image processing we use on our movies.”

“I’ve messed with plenty of good 3rd party tools,” Johnson continues. “But this is an elegant one-stop-shop, it just takes beautiful shots with Steve’s special sauce processing. You can fine-tune the image in the app (with color, exposure, grain, and halation tools) and export it to your camera roll.”

As Johnson explains, Chromagraph Camera lets smartphone photographers process RAW files and allows them to shoot photos with manual controls, such as shutter speed.

The app also allows users to import RAW images that have already been shot, process them in the app, and then export them.

The app aims to recreate filmic looks. Yedlin is well-placed to oversee such a project because he has researched color science extensively. Fast Company notes that in 2015, he gave a demonstration showing how film looks can be recreated using RAW camera data.

In fact, Yedlin has done just that for Johnson’s movies, creating a series of color-grading scripts to make their productions feel like they were shot on celluloid. It was this work that led to Chromagraph Camera.

Johnson tells The Verge that he is a film photographer “nerd” and is often seen on set with a Leica M6.

“The reality is, as much as I love my Leica, as much as I love my other gear, it’s a pain having a camera on your shoulder, or a massive backpack with four cameras in it,” Johnson tells the tech publication. “And I always have my phone with me.”

Chromagraph Camera is available from the App Store for $13.

#9178. As Route 66 shifts into its centennial year, preservation efforts accelerate

Highway star: in New Mexico, Albuquerque’s Route 66 Visitor Center, which opened last April, is home to restored roadside signs from along the 2,500-mile route Courtesy of Friends of the Orphan Signs

US Route 66 officially started on 11 November 1926 with the launch of the nation’s first federal highway system. With the spread of affordable automobiles after the Second World War, it became a destination. A unique vernacular culture formed along its almost 2,500 miles running through eight states from Chicago, Illinois to Santa Monica, California, from neon signs enticing travellers to themed motels to roadside attractions with concrete and fibreglass sculptures.

Route 66 was decommissioned in 1985, with the new highways bypassing its Art Deco service stations and mid-century diners. Now, 100 years after its debut, there are efforts across the country to preserve what survives from what was once the “Main Street of America”.

“We want to let people outside of Route 66 know that it’s more than what you think it is,” says Rhys Martin, manager of the Preserve Route 66 Initiative at the National Trust for Historic Preservation. “Most people think of ’57 Chevys and cheeseburgers and Marilyn Monroe, and there’s a lot of that, but there’s so much more. It ties together so many diverse cultures, from Native American to African American. In my home state of Oklahoma, it goes through the Asian District [in Oklahoma City], which sprung up around Vietnamese refugees during the war. In West Hollywood, Route 66 has a huge LGBTQ presence.”

Grants from the Preserve Route 66 Initiative reflect that range of history, which is often overlooked in the nostalgia for its Americana. There are structural repair needs, like at the Fanning 66 Outpost in Cuba, Missouri, which hosts a 42ft-high rocking chair (the world’s largest until 2015), as well as storytelling projects, such as mapping Native American experiences along the corridor, as it passes through many tribal and ancestral lands yet has had little representation of their voices. Care for the road extends to the scarce sections of its original pavement. Through local advocacy, what is known as the Ribbon Road in Ottawa County, Oklahoma, which has the last segment of a 9ft-wide design made for Model Ts, was partially protected from resurfacing this year.

“You might think a pavement’s not art, but when you get out and look at it, especially compared to what it is today, it is very different,” Martin says. “I have come to really appreciate it from a craftsmanship perspective, but also a longevity perspective. These are the same roads that the Model Ts went west on during the Dust Bowl to seek a better life, and the fact that I get to drive these same roads tells a story.”

Advocacy is under way to give National Historic Trail designation to Route 66, with a bipartisan bill introduced last year. Martin notes that Route 66 is now similar to how it was before 1926, when it was a loose network of roads, and this legislation would help bring together its fragmented parts.

“It gets people to sit at the same table, like the state Route 66 associations, the National Park Service and the Department of Transportation, so that we can find ways to work together for corridor-wide initiatives and to help elevate preservation needs,” he says. “The corridor continues to evolve, and buildings are threatened all the time with demolition or augmentation beyond recognition, and being designated as a National Historic Trail is not a roadblock. But it is something to say, this is important and we need to take care when the fabric of the road might be forever altered.”

Coca Cola painting on a brick wall, along Route 66 in Stroud, Oklahoma Courtesy National Trust for Historic Preservation

Local groups, municipalities and individuals are stewarding Route 66’s relics. Martin is also the president of the Oklahoma Route 66 Association, which is restoring a U-Haul painted by the late artist Bob Waldmire, who illustrated maps and postcards of the road’s built and natural wonders. The city of Catoosa in Oklahoma acquired the beloved roadside Blue Whale in 2020 from the family of Hugh S. Davis, who in 1972 sculpted the 80ft-long attraction from concrete as a gift for his wife. Last May, a new Blue Whale Visitor Center opened with retro illuminated signage.

The city of Albuquerque opened a Route 66 Visitor Center last April and its park features a collection of restored roadside signs. Among them is the first major project from the Friends of the Orphan Signs (FOS), an organisation that since 2010 has worked on revitalising abandoned signs, particularly in Albuquerque’s underserved neighbourhoods.

Lindsey Fromm, the executive director of FOS, says that many of these signs are for places that were razed during the city’s removal of derelict buildings: “There were areas of Route 66 with dozens of towering empty signs.”

Most Route 66 sign restorations return them to their former glory; FOS reimagines them as public art. Revivir (2012) at the new visitor centre was created with students who designed visuals responding to local nature that were bordered with purple neon.

“While artists lead these sign projects, they will collaborate with communities, archives, the surrounding environment, or will collect histories and stories to create the work that is displayed, so that it speaks to the immediate moment and surrounding community who live, work and travel by the sign,” Fromm says.

Projects like this are not just about preserving places for tourists but Route 66’s role in daily life. These grassroots and national efforts recognise that even though it is no longer a main thoroughfare, it is still a vital place of connection from the Midwest to the Pacific, for communities both urban and rural, and between the visitors and residents brought together on their journeys.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation is helping 30 congregations shore up their buildings and share their stories, with their communities and the world

The Hendrick I. Lott House in southeast Brooklyn—former home to a family of enslavers who later made it a stop on the Underground Railroad—will undergo a major preservation and renovation project next year

Selma’s long-abandoned Edistone Hotel, witness to 170 years of African American history, was recently saved by a non-profit devoted to protecting Black historical sites

The two-year grant Conserving Black Modernism extends the foundation's larger initiative to protect Modernist architecture

#9177. Camera Traps Catch Newly Discovered Howler Monkey Crossing Rope Bridge

Camera Traps Catch Newly Discovered Howler Monkey Crossing Rope Bridge

A new species of howler monkey has been discovered in Brazil and has already been spied crossing life-saving rope bridges built by conservationists.

When a new species is discovered in 2026, there are often two viable explanations for why it took so long to be found. First, it is extremely similar to known species and can only be disentangled through complex, time-consuming genetic analysis. Second, the species lives in such a remote place and in such sparse numbers that it has simply never been observed before.

In the latter case, the species is usually already facing an existential threat. Today, to evade detection for so long typically means there are barely any individuals alive.

That’s part of what makes this story about a newly described howler monkey species so special. Yes, it is in low numbers, but heartwarming and effective conservation efforts were already underway long before the species was officially described.

As National Geographic explains, one of the world’s newest howler monkey species, Alouatta matogrossensis, was recently spotted in thousands of camera-trap photos in Brazil. There’s even a fun video clip in Nat Geo‘s story.

Projeto Reconecta is an incredible organization that builds rope bridges across dangerous and busy areas in Brazil, enabling monkeys to safely climb their way across. Many camera traps are set up along these bridges, providing invaluable data to scientists. Most of the subjects in these photos are well-known species, such as capuchins and titi monkeys.

However, when researchers saw Alouatta matogrossensis in their photos, they were blown away.

“We were all amazed that we were providing safe crossing opportunities for a new monkey species,” explains National Geographic Explorer and ecologist Fernanda Abra, leader of Projeto Reconecta.

An international team of scientists recently published their findings in Communications Biology. Study co-author Romina Batista, an evolutionary biologist at the National Institute of Amazonian Research, called the images “super important.”

While it’s great news that Alouatta matogrossensis is using the rope bridges, primatologist, explorer, and study co-author Jean Boubli says that the newly discovered monkeys are likely in “grave danger.”

“They’re found in a place where the forest is at its worst shape in the whole of Brazil,” Boubli says.

“The cities are getting bigger, so there is more agriculture, agriculture fields, cars everywhere,” Abra continues. As National Geographic writes, that means an increased risk of primates being struck and killed by vehicles.

Alouatta matogrossensis is either “endangered or critically endangered,” Boubli adds.

Boubli, who has been exploring the Amazon and studying primates for 30 years, continues to be surprised by the biodiversity of the region. Researchers have identified 16 howler monkey species so far, including a second one detailed in the new study.

Abra’s rope bridges have provided safe crossings for three recently discovered monkey species so far, including the endangered Alta Floresta titi monkey described in 2019, Schneider’s marmoset discovered in 2021, and now the new howler monkey.

What new species might cross Abra’s rope bridges next?

#9176. William N. Copley "X-Rated (1972–1974)" @ Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin

Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin, is pleased to announce X-Rated (1972–1974), a solo exhibition of paintings and works on paper by William N. Copley. This is the fourth presentation of the artist’s work at the gallery, and the show will be on view through April 22, 2026.

Copley came to painting from an unusual position. He had ambitions to become a writer before becoming a painter, and, for a brief period in the late 1940s, he co-founded and operated a gallery in Beverly Hills that focused on the Surrealists. The Copley Galleries – which he ran with his brother-in-law, the artist John Ployardt – brought him into close contact with exiled Surrealists such as Man Ray, Max Ernst and Marcel Duchamp, as well as the dealer Alexander Iolas, who encouraged him to pursue his nascent art practice. Adopting the signature CPLY around the time the gallery closed, he debuted his first exhibition at a bookstore in Los Angeles in 1951, shortly before he moved to France.Even though he was a generation younger than the Surrealists, Copley’s work is deeply informed by the movement on a conceptual and personal level. While his bold black outlines and self-taught figurative style recall comics and Pop art, Copley approached painting with a literary sensibility, using narrative strategies that both embodied Surrealist principles and drove the structural evolution of his compositions. Like many Surrealists, Copley embraced humour, psychology and eroticism as fundamental to his creative process, yet his engagement with overtly sexual subjects went far beyond the playful eroticism of his peers.On view in the exhibition are works from Copley’s prolific ‘X-Rated’ series, created between 1972 and 1975, and first exhibited in 1974 in an eponymous show at the New York Cultural Center. This body of work draws on erotic imagery and ritualised motifs from adult magazines, seeking, in the artist’s own words, to ‘break through the barrier of pornography into the area of joy.’ 1In a decade when the sale of hardcore pornography was still illegal in the United States, Copley would buy ‘adult magazines’ under the counter, using them as a source for inventive figurative and narrative paintings that explored eroticism, sexual politics and the pursuit of pleasure. The artist was able to convey a wide range of tone in the ‘X-Rated’ paintings: some, such as The Seven Year Itch, 1973, are tender; others, including  Viridiana, 1973, are exuberant; and almost all of them are openly humorous. Underscoring the open-endedness of sexual expression, Copley stated: ‘That’s what makes sex so much fun: since nobody really understands it, the possibilities for originality are endless.’ 2Copley typically produced two stages of preparatory drawings before starting a painting: an initial, small-scale study, followed by a larger version in which he refined the composition, introduced changes, and heightened the work’s pictorial dynamism. The resulting paintings maintain a deliberately slapdash style, with figures treated loosely rather than meticulously rendered. The exhibition makes this developmental process visible through multiple pairings of preparatory drawings and completed paintings, including Calcutta, 1973, and its counterpart Untitled, 1973.Scenes of copulations and orgies are set against vivid, brightly coloured backgrounds animated by bold, geometric patterns, making them almost ‘too artful to be libidinous, let alone lascivious’, as critic James R. Mellow has remarked. 3 It is both this treatment of the backgrounds and the contorted, entwined bodies with their attenuated limbs and schematic outlines that has prompted critics to draw a link between Copley and Henri Matisse more than once. Yet, while depictions of the nude and sexual imagery throughout art history have traditionally relied on suggestion and idealisation, Copley presents the sexual act directly, leaving nothing to the imagination.With titles borrowed from Hollywood movies such as Les Quatre Cent Coups, The Exorcist or Tobacco Road, Copley tempered the shock of the pornographic image through comic playfulness and pop cultural sensibility. Manifesting a Surrealist disjunction, the movies rarely align explicitly with the images’ content, but the titles nevertheless set in motion a cascade of associations for the viewer. The title of the series, likewise, draws on terminology from the film industry: until the 1990s, the film-classification term ‘X-rated’ was used in the US for films only suitable for adults. Despite the cautionary notices that some visitors might find the subject matter offensive, the 1974 exhibition at the Cultural Center – curated by the newly appointed and strikingly progressive director Mario Amaya – received a notably positive critical response. Art in America writer Peter Schjeldahl hailed the presentation as a ‘uniformly gorgeous exhibition,’ noting that it marked ‘a highly satisfying development in Copley’s work’. 4The ‘X-Rated’ series represents a singular chapter in Copley’s oeuvre, deliberately set apart from the prevailing currents of the early-1970s art scene. Even in today’s uncensored and image-saturated world, Copley’s suggestive canvases retain a subversive charge. By merging art and eroticism, Copley challenged conservative norms and rejected the notion of artistic neutrality, clearing away moralistic constraints in favour of directness and humour.
