A Creative Agent, generative gap-fill, and a new approach to colour grading lead the way at Adobe Max.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Premiere Pro is getting Adobe's Creative Agent, and it looks set to take a lot of the grunt work out of editing. In a pre-Adobe Max 2026 demo, I saw it apply effects across every clip in a sequence, track masked subjects through frames, and adjust colour and exposure across an entire sequence at once. The use-case argument for more AI, now Agentic AI, in creative work, and particularly here in video editing, continues to be a replacement for repetitive jobs that most editors would happily hand off.

That, of course, raises questions about who used to be handed those repetitive but creative jobs and whether those roles are now no longer viable. But for many creatives, particularly freelancers, handing process work to an AI agent is likely very enticing.

So let's take a closer look at the new Generative Media Tool for those looking to speed up their workflows. Instead of jumping between apps and AI services, editors can generate video, sound effects, soundscapes, and music directly in Premiere's timeline. You can select a range, describe what you need, and add the generated media as an editable clip, so you don't have to break your editing flow to get the material you need. The demo was certainly impressive.

More controversially, Adobe is also bringing supported third-party AI models into the workflow, giving editors more choice in how they generate video but also opening up Adobe's app ecosystem to external AI models such as Kling and Seedance 2.5, which have greyer areas than Adobe Firefly. More practically, a new Generative Remove tool, currently in beta, can delete unwanted objects from a video frame and shot, filling the space with realistic detail, even figuring out where related shadows of a now-omitted object should be removed.

Color Mode is another big part of the Premiere Pro update. It's a dedicated colour-grading workspace that reshapes the interface around the job, with editable Style Presets that can apply a consistent look across an entire sequence. They're a bit like traditional Looks, only you can get inside them and adjust the individual elements.

You can also work across groups of clips, making it easier to fix inconsistencies between shots without grading each one individually. New on-screen HUDs provide feedback as you make adjustments, helping you stay focused on the footage rather than a wall of sliders.

Adobe is also expanding its AI-powered audio tools, including Enhance Audio, Separate Crosstalk, and Separate Sound Source, to clean up dialogue and separate elements in a mix.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Premiere Mobile is getting the Creative Agent in private beta, bringing agentic editing to phones. It can turn footage into editable first cuts, make changes using natural-language prompts and help refine videos while keeping the creator in control.

Adobe is also adding hundreds of thousands of licensed music tracks from Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group to Premiere Mobile on iPhone, with Android coming soon. There's a catch: the music is licensed for personal, non-commercial videos, while commercial projects can continue to use Adobe Stock Audio.

Finally, Premiere is included in Adobe's Local MCP integrations preview. This allows third-party agents to work with native Premiere project files locally, alongside Photoshop, Illustrator and After Effects. Importantly, sequences, bins and other project elements remain editable, meaning you can step in and make changes yourself.

As ever with these tools, the real test will be how much of the creative process editors are comfortable handing over.

#9155. Hiroshi Sato’s Art Against Enshittification

“Insincere ironic detachment is abundant,” the Bay Area artist told Hyperallergic. “What is niche now are sincere depictions of the present.”

SAN FRANCISCO — What does reality look like in the age of AI? For the San Francisco-based painter Hiroshi Sato, representational figurative painting is the antidote to our rapid loss of touch with what’s real and what isn’t. His stylistic blend of Bay Area Figurative Movement stylings and Edward Hopper-esque compositions creates an uneasy and uncanny portrait of what it feels like to be alive today — and might offer a way out of the simulacrum we all seem trapped in.

But Sato wasn’t always motivated by a desire to return to the real. He credits the COVID-19 pandemic with shifting his outlook on both politics and painting.

“Before COVID, my practice wasn’t about subject matter at all,” he told me when I visited him in his cramped Mission District studio in San Francisco, one of the last such buildings in the neighborhood artists were pushed out of during the dot-com boom. “When the pandemic happened, I realized that you can’t just keep making work that appears to be immune from time and what’s happening around you.”

#9154. $160,000 Hans Arp Sculpture Stolen From Art Cologne

“S’élevant (Rising)” (1962) was snatched from Gallery Ludorff's booth on November 8.

German police are seeking answers about the theft of Hans (Jean) Arp's “S’élevant (Rising)” (1962) from Gallery Ludorff's booth at Art Cologne, which went missing from its plinth on the last day of the blue-chip fair on Sunday, November 8, between 4:55pm and 5:10pm.

Since the fair kicked off on November 5, Arp's work had been sitting atop a plinth at the Düsseldorf gallery's booth, sandwiched between two paintings by Ernst Wilhelm Nay. Four employees were at the stand on November 8 and immediately notified the North Rhine-Westphalia State Police upon noticing that the unbolted sculpture, which is valued at €145,000 (~$160,000), had gone missing. As it remains unclear who made off with the 28-centimeter-tall (~11 in) sculpture, police are seeking any information or photographs from visitors or staffers that could aid in the investigation.

#9152. German museum returns Slevogt painting to heirs of Nazi-persecuted collector

Max Slevogt's Paradiesvögel (Birds of Paradise, 1900) © Ketterer Kunst

A painting by the German Impressionist painter Max Slevogt, which has been restituted to the heirs of Eduard Fuchs—a collector, Communist and writer who fled Nazi Germany with his Jewish wife—will be auctioned next month. Slevogt's Paradiesvögel (Birds of Paradise, 1900), was acquired by the Von der Heydt-Museum in Wuppertal, western Germany, in 2006 and following an investigation that began in 2020 was approved for restitution by the Wuppertal city council on 13 July 2026. Paradiesvögel will be offered at Ketterer Kunst's 5 December Day Sale with an estimate of €40,000–€60,000.

Given the large number of heirs a sale was the only option, Ketterer Kunst's head of communications Anja Häse tells The Art Newspaper. The heirs consigned the painting once the restitution was completed, she adds. Another work by Slevogt from Fuchs’s collection, Don Quichotte und die Schafherde (Don Quixote and the Flock of Sheep, 1907) is also included in the auction with an estimate of €20,000–€30,000. According to Ketterer Kunst's provenance information, a settlement was reached between the current private owners and Fuchs's heirs in 2026, allowing the work to be offered at auction free of restitution claims. The terms of the “amicable restitution” have not been disclosed.

Max Slevogt's Don Quichotte und die Schafherde (Don Quixote and the Flock of Sheep, 1907) © Ketterer Kunst

Fuchs's collection was confiscated by the Nazis but later released. In 1937, he was forced to sell works from the collection to pay a punitive emigration tax imposed by the Nazi authorities. Paradiesvögel was auctioned in Berlin in June 1937 and acquired by the art dealer Hildebrand Gurlitt, passing to Fritz Slevogt in 1939.

Paradiesvögel was included in a sale at Kunsthaus Lempertz in December 2004, estimated at €100,000-€120,000, but went unsold. According to Meyer, the work remained in the auction house’s custody afterwards and was subsequently exhibited at the Von der Heydt-Museum in 2005. The museum then purchased the painting through the auction house in 2006 for €120,000. Meyer says that while the painting's provenance was documented in the 2004 auction catalogue, the museum can no longer establish whether a provenance check was carried out before the acquisition or how thoroughly it was assessed. She also confirmed that the museum is not considering any legal action against Kunsthaus Lempertz regarding due diligence on the painting.

The provenance investigation began after Fuchs's heirs contacted the institution in 2020, the museum's press officer Marion Meyer tells The Art Newspaper. The research drew on a wider project, supported by the German Lost Art Foundation, to reconstruct Eduard and Margarete Fuchs's collection.

“Restituting Max Slevogt's Paradiesvögel means losing a painting, but we gain something far more important: the certainty that we have acted responsibly towards history,” the Von der Heydt-Museum's director Roland Mönig says in a press statement. He describes provenance research as “an essential part of our work”.

In 2024, the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart restituted Slevogt's Der verlorene Sohn (The Prodigal Son, 1899) to Fuchs's heirs. The triptych was sold at Ketterer Kunst later that year.

#9151. Human Rights Orgs Denounce Egypt's Arrest of Mada Masr Editor Lina Attalah

Attalah was accused of publishing false news and operating without a license amid Egyptian authorities’ extensive crackdown on independent press.

Prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, co-founder and editor-in-chief of Egypt's independent news outlet Mada Masr, is facing a one-year prison sentence among other penalties in a targeted crackdown on press freedom.

Summoned to court in Cairo last month on charges of publishing false news and operating the news site without a license, Attalah learned during the proceedings that she had been handed a year-long sentence in absentia on similar charges in 2024 without her knowledge.

Human rights and press freedom organizations, including Reporters Without Borders, Human Rights Watch, and the International Federation for Human Rights, have publicly condemned the charges against the journalist and Mada Masr, decrying her prosecution as a “Kafkaesque miscarriage of justice.”

#9150. After the Midterms, the Real Work for Arts and Culture Begins

Democratic leaders need to understand that cultural funding cannot stop at large museums and institutions; it must reach the people whose labor makes it possible.

In the afterglow of the blue-nami, those of us who make, organize, fund, and sustain cultural life are feeling a twinge of hope. But I find myself slipping into a spiral of anxiety as the everyday reality of economic precarity sets back in. Our newly elected Democratic congressional leaders have an opportunity to change that reality — pushing back against Trump is necessary — but it cannot be the full extent of their ambition.

As a curator and the co-director of an arts nonprofit, I’ve been asked what the results mean for the so-called “art world.” My first response was cynical: “not much.” At least not immediately. An election does not directly restore a canceled grant or pay an artist’s rent. And even a return to the funding landscape that existed before Trump took office in 2025 would leave us with a system that was already failing the people expected to sustain it.

Instead, the midterm election results should serve as an opening to hold Democrats in Congress accountable for making arts and cultural life materially sustainable, not simply to defend an inadequate system from further attack. That mandate concerns whose histories are told, who gets paid to make art, and who gets to define the country’s future. It also concerns whether the people doing that work can afford to keep going.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Adobe has announced an expanded partnership with Google at Adobe MAX 2026, and while the announcement is heavy on AI jargon, there implications for creatives could be interesting.

Perhaps most exciting is a collaboration with Google DeepMind to develop new AI editing capabilities for Photoshop. The companies are exploring a customised Google image model that could allow users to make near-real-time edits using text prompts, switching between variations without disrupting their workflow. In theory, that could make generative editing feel less like a frustrating cycle of prompting and waiting, and more like working with a traditional Photoshop tool. The catch? It's still exploratory, with no release date announced.

“Adobe’s mission is to empower everyone to create, and our AI innovations are helping more people express their ideas and create in ways that amplify their voice, while maintaining creative control,” said Anil Chakravarthy, president and incoming CEO of Adobe. “Our expanded partnership combines Google’s frontier AI with Adobe’s industry-leading creative and productivity tools at global scale, enabling us to deliver differentiated experiences and bring Adobe’s innovations to more people across Adobe and Google products.”

Meanwhile, Adobe is bringing its creative tools to Google's AI Mode in Search, potentially allowing users to go straight from searching for inspiration to creating something without opening a separate app.

Adobe is also expanding its integrations with Gemini and Gemini Enterprise, enabling users to enhance images, customise designs and work with PDFs through conversational prompts. For designers churning out multiple versions of campaign assets, for example, that could be a genuine time-saver.

Perhaps the most interesting aspect of the announcement, though, is what it suggests about Adobe's direction. Rather than expecting creatives to work exclusively within its own apps, it seems Adobe increasingly wants its tools accessible wherever people are already working, such as Google Workspace.

#9148. Nothing but a single joint holds together Dado furniture

Berlin studio Allen Kaufmann Architekten has adapted a traditional woodworking joint to create a flat-pack range that can be assembled completely without tools – and it’s been voted furniture design of the year by Dezeen readers.

No glue, screws, brackets or other fasteners are used in the Dado tables and shelves.

Instead, their solid-timber construction is held together using only one deceptively simple type of joint: a narrow trench cut across the length of one piece of wood so another can slot into it.

Known as a dado or housing joint, it has been a fixture of woodworking for thousands of years.

But Allen Kaufmann Architekten has reimagined this traditional technique as the only thing holding up an entire self-supporting furniture range that can be easily flat-packed, assembled, demounted and repaired.

“I started with the traditional dado cut, a simple groove cut into timber, and asked whether that basic operation could become an entire structural system rather than simply a joint,” explained studio co-founder Justin Allen.

His patented joint, developed over several years of prototyping, turns dado cuts on their head – or more precisely, at a 45-degree angle – so they can be used to join not just two pieces of wood but four.

This allows a vertical element, a horizontal element and two diagonal braces to lock together at a single point through simple geometry.

“Visually, it has something of a post-and-beam construction, with intersecting diagonal bracing, almost like the inside of a timber barn,” the architect explained. “But the geometry and the way all four elements meet are specific to Dado, giving the joint its own distinct appearance.”

So far, Allen has used this same logic to create a table and a modular shelving system, using a limited set of repeated parts.

As Allen sees it, this offers a more elegant solution to current joinery systems. Furniture with permanent fixings is cumbersome, expensive and emissions-intensive to transport, he argues, while traditional flat-pack systems rely on different screws, brackets and fittings that can be lost or damaged.

In both cases, the joints limit how often and how easily the furniture can be disassembled and reused, which can lead to an otherwise functional piece being abandoned.

With Dado, Allen has avoided the need for fixings and left the joints themselves exposed, in the hope that the furniture’s owner will be able to understand how it works and how it might be maintained.

“The connection remains visible, so the joint becomes the detail, the structure, the assembly and ultimately the design,” he explained.

Each of the range’s standard components is CNC milled with machine precision. This allows the whole range to be produced by a single workshop anywhere in the world – another win in the transport department.

Dado was named furniture design of the year in this year’s Dezeen Awards public vote and is now in the running to be crowned overall winner by a jury of leading industry figures including Norman Foster, Michael Anastassiades and Jaime Hayon.

There, it is up against projects from Tom Fereday, Yabu Pushelberg, String Furniture and more.

#9147. How to Free the Art World From Its Neoliberal Capture

In “The Battleground of Art,” curator and activist Marco Baravalle dissects the art establishment's co-optation of radical politics and uplifts the stories of collectives that resist it.

We first met Marco Baravalle in 2015 at the 56th Venice Biennale, All the World’s Futures, when we were organizing with the Gulf Labor Coalition. The group and our autonomous direct-action wing, Global Ultra Luxury Faction (G.U.L.F.), had been invited by curator Okwui Enwezor to present our research and organizing against migrant worker exploitation in the construction of the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi. An artist boycott was underway, direct actions were escalating, and days earlier, on May 1, we had shut down the Guggenheim Museum in New York City.

Through Baravalle, a longtime researcher, curator, and activist, we encountered a network of autonomous spaces in Venice and Milan. These were not simply cultural centers; they formed the infrastructure for collective organizing, resistance, and enacting other worlds.

Eleven years later, The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism (2026) extends this praxis into an important and timely call to action. Drawing on his two decades of experience, Baravalle offers what we have called movement-generated theory and practice, rooted in the dialectic of doing and knowing. The book confronts the neoliberal capture of the art world, while also excavating histories and practices of abolition and autonomy that offer other possibilities.

Compound interest is often called the eighth wonder of the world, and for good reason. It is the mathematical force that turns consistent, modest investing into life-changing wealth — and it is the foundation of every financial independence plan.

Here is the core concept. Simple interest earns a return only on your original deposit. If you invest $10,000 at 7% simple interest, you earn $700 per year — every year, forever, on the same $10,000 base. After 30 years, you would have $31,000.

Compound interest earns a return on your original deposit plus all the interest previously earned. In Year 1, you earn $700 on your $10,000. In Year 2, you earn 7% on $10,700 — that is $749. In Year 3, you earn 7% on $11,449 — that is $801. Each year, your interest earns its own interest, and the growth accelerates.

After 30 years of compound interest at 7%, your $10,000 grows to approximately $76,123 — more than double the $31,000 from simple interest. And that is with a single $10,000 deposit and no additional contributions.

The difference starts small and then explodes. In the first 10 years, compound interest adds only $2,672 more than simple interest. In the last 10 years (year 20 to 30), it adds over $30,000 more. This accelerating curve is why time in the market matters more than almost any other factor in building wealth.

Investing $500 per month at a 7% average annual return — roughly the inflation-adjusted historical return of the S&P 500 — produces dramatically different results depending on how long you invest. After 10 years: $86,500. After 20 years: $260,500. After 30 years: $567,000. You contribute $180,000 of your own money over 30 years. Compound interest adds $387,000 — more than double your contributions. Time is the multiplier that no amount of additional savings can replace.

The compound interest formula is straightforward once you understand the components:

For a $10,000 investment at 7% compounded monthly for 30 years:

A = 10,000 x (1 + 0.07/12)^(12 x 30) = 10,000 x (1.00583)^360 = $81,165

Notice this is higher than the $76,123 from annual compounding — more frequent compounding produces slightly more growth, though the difference is modest.

The jump from annual to monthly compounding is meaningful. The jump from monthly to daily is negligible. Most bank accounts and investment returns compound daily or monthly, so you are already getting nearly the maximum benefit.

The Rule of 72 is the single most useful mental math shortcut in personal finance. Divide 72 by your expected annual return to estimate how many years it takes to double your money.

At a 7% real return, your money doubles every 10 years. A $100,000 portfolio at age 25 becomes $200,000 at 35, $400,000 at 45, and $800,000 at 55 — even with zero additional contributions. This is why starting early is the single most powerful financial decision you can make.

The following table shows how different monthly contribution amounts grow over time at a 7% average annual return (roughly the inflation-adjusted long-term return of the US stock market). These numbers assume you start with $0 and contribute consistently every month.

Notice the pattern: the growth in the third decade dwarfs the first two decades combined. At $1,000 per month, you accumulate $173,000 in the first 10 years but $613,000 in the last 10 years — with the same monthly contribution. This is compound interest in its most powerful phase.

The 7% figure used above is already adjusted for historical inflation (the nominal S&P 500 return has averaged roughly 10%, minus approximately 3% average inflation). This means the projections above represent real purchasing power — $567,000 in 30 years would buy roughly what $567,000 buys today.

If you use a nominal return of 10% instead, the numbers look even more dramatic, but they overstate your future purchasing power. Always use inflation-adjusted returns (6-7%) for retirement planning and real purchasing power comparisons.

Consider two investors. Investor A starts investing $500 per month at age 25 and stops at age 35 — investing for only 10 years, then letting it grow untouched until age 65. Investor B waits until age 35 and invests $500 per month every month from 35 to 65 — investing for 30 years.

Investor A contributes one-third the money and ends up with more at 65. The 10-year head start gave compound interest enough time to overcome the difference. This is not a trick — it is the fundamental math of compounding. Every year you delay costs you more than the money you eventually invest.

The single most important factor in compound interest is time, not amount. Even $100 per month started today beats $500 per month started five years from now over a long enough timeline. Open a brokerage account or increase your 401(k) contribution today.

Pro tip: Automate your contributions so they happen before you see the money in your checking account.

The historical 7-10% average return comes from broad stock market index funds. A total US stock market fund or S&P 500 fund with an expense ratio below 0.10% gives you the full benefit of compound growth without high fees eroding your returns.

When you get a raise, increase your monthly investment by at least half the raise amount. This prevents lifestyle inflation from consuming your additional income and accelerates compound growth.

Pro tip: A 3% annual raise invested means your contributions grow exponentially alongside your investment returns.

Set all your accounts to automatically reinvest dividends. Dividend reinvestment is compound interest within compound interest — your dividends buy more shares, which generate more dividends, which buy more shares.

Market downturns are not a reason to sell — they are the cost of admission for long-term compound growth. Every major market crash in history has been followed by recovery and new highs. Pulling money out during a downturn and reinvesting later is the most reliable way to destroy compound interest.

Pro tip: If seeing your balance drop causes panic, check your portfolio less frequently. Quarterly or annually is enough.

Simple interest is calculated only on your original principal. Compound interest is calculated on your principal plus all previously earned interest. Over long periods, the difference is enormous — $10,000 at 7% for 30 years grows to $31,000 with simple interest but $76,123 with compound interest.

More frequent compounding produces slightly higher returns, but the difference is small. Monthly compounding at 7% on $10,000 for 30 years yields $81,165 versus $76,123 for annual compounding — a difference of about 6.6%. Most investment accounts compound daily or when dividends are reinvested, so you are already receiving near-optimal compounding.

Yes. Compound interest (more accurately, compound growth) applies to any investment account where your returns are reinvested. In a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account invested in index funds, your gains generate additional gains. Tax-advantaged accounts like Roth IRAs are especially powerful because the compounding occurs entirely tax-free.

The S&P 500 has returned approximately 10% annually in nominal terms over the past century. Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7%. For conservative planning, use 6-7% to account for inflation. For nominal calculations (not inflation-adjusted), use 9-10%. Using rates above 10% for long-term projections is overly optimistic for a diversified portfolio.

Yes — and the math is surprisingly accessible. Investing $1,000 per month at a 7% real return reaches $1,134,000 in 30 years (you contribute $360,000, compound interest adds $774,000). At $500 per month, you reach $567,000 in 30 years. The key variables are consistent contribution, a reasonable return, and patience.

Compound interest is the mathematical engine behind financial independence. The FI community uses compound growth to accumulate 25x their annual expenses in invested assets (the 4% rule). By saving 50%+ of income and investing in index funds that compound at 7-10% annually, FIRE practitioners can reach financial independence in 10-17 years rather than the traditional 40-year career.

Compound interest is the most powerful wealth-building force available to ordinary investors. The math is unambiguous: $500 per month at 7% becomes $567,000 in 30 years, with compound interest contributing more than twice what you personally invest. The two factors you control — how much you invest and how long you stay invested — matter far more than picking the "right" stocks or timing the market. Start today, invest in low-cost index funds, reinvest all dividends, and do not interrupt the compounding. Time is your greatest asset, and every year you wait costs more than you think.

#9145. Print Center and Women’s Studio Workshop Name New Leaders

Plus, SITE Santa Fe artists announced, awards for Lorna Simpson and Wolfgang Tillmans, and Penske Media partners with Amazon … because of course.

Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

New York's Print Center, home to programs and exhibitions celebrating all the art that's pressed, proofed, and published, announced Yukiko Yamagata as its new executive director this week.

Her professional profile doesn't immediately scream “print nerd”: Yamagata most recently served as deputy director at Creative Time and previously worked at the Open Society Foundations, where she led a $15.8 million arts and culture fellowship program for socially engaged artists. But one of her earliest roles in the 1990s was as a senior curatorial assistant in the photo department at the Whitney Museum of American Art, and she is a current board member of Women Photograph, an organization focused on equitable practices in photojournalism and visual media.

Yamagata succeeds Judy Hecker, who announced her decision to step down earlier this year after a decade in the role, and is now executive director emerita.

The Women's Studio Workshop in Rosendale, New York, dedicated to the printing arts as well as papermaking, bookbinding, photography, and more, has named Natalie Renganeschi as its fourth-ever executive director in the organization's 52-year history.

Renganeschi's career at WSW began in 2018, when she joined as a part-time employee while working as a high school art teacher. Now, she will oversee the nonprofit's major campus expansion, including the relaunch of its ceramics center.

“My path to leadership hasn’t been a traditional one, but it’s rooted in the ethos of WSW,” Renganeschi said in a statement. “Just as our mediums are steeped in process and the history of craft, working here is a sustained act of communal learning that allows for growth to come from below and within.”

#9144. Library by Collective Architecture breathes new life into Scottish high street

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson

The conversion of a dilapidated high-street building into a public library in Paisley, Scotland, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.

The film forms part of a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are introduced to Paisley Central Library, designed by Scottish studio Collective Architecture to serve as a welcoming community space with reading areas, event spaces and a study room.

According to studio director Ewan Imrie, Paisley Central Library was conceived as a civic space for “people to dwell”.

“The client was very clear from the outset that the building had to be as welcoming to all different types of people from all aspects of society,” Imrie said.

“Encouraging people to dwell was the most important thing and if they pick up a book and read it then that’s a bonus.”

Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be announced on 26 November.

Comprising three reuse projects, RIAS said this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “important conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Paisley Central Library is the Edinburgh Futures Institute by Bennetts Associates and the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by Studio Octopi.

Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

It's trying to strike a difficult balancing act.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When KitBash bought ArtStation, it pledged the address users concerns about the flood of AI content on the digital art platform. It took the first step back in September, when it turned on 'NoAI' for uploads by default, marking them as unavailable for AI training.

Now a new update introduces an attempt to police generative AI content along with more complete AI declarations and more control over filtering. The aim is to make it easier to users to control what they see, but it's got a mixed response from artists so far.

We're introducing the next phase of generative AI content controls. Creators will have clearer AI declaration requirements when publishing, and AI filtering is now on by default, with options that give you finer control. Learn what's changing → https://t.co/cuHmcoAuhw https://t.co/64PevA0XjmNovember 9, 2026

When publishing content on ArtStation, users will now be asked to declare whether generative AI was used in the creation of the piece. Creators can identify their work as primarily generative AI, mixed generative AI and non-generative methods or 100% non-generative.

This relies on users being upfront, and ArtStation says that most are. However, it's recognised that there is a problem with people uploading AI-generated content without flagging it as such.

That leads to the second aspect of the latest update, which is a dedicated channel for reporting AI content. If users come across artwork they think is AI-generated but which isn't labelled, they can report it. ArtStation says that every report will help improve its AI filtering for the whole community.

Users also get more control over what they're shown: they can choose whether to hide declared generative AI content, or to allow mixed generative and non-generative workflows, and they can adjust how aggressively ArtStation filters content based on user reports of suspected generative AI.

The 'Strict' setting hides artwork when just a few reports suggest it may be AI-generated. 'Balanced' filters it out when there’s a moderate level of reports and 'Loose' removes it only when user signals are strongest. By default, the filter will be set to not show any project declared as AI-generated, tagged with 'CreatedwithAI' or tagged with generative AI tools, and suspected as AI will be set to strict.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The platform risks becoming useless if it's impossible to find interesting work because of the sheer volume of low-quality AI-generated content. Many users have welcomed the latest update as a move in the right direction, while others have raised doubts about how effective the measures it will be.

There's a strong reliance on user moderation, which will depend on users accurately identifying AI art. Some may still go undetected completely, while the 'Strict' filtering could remove work falsely identified as AI.

It's not yet clear if artists will be notified if their work is flagged or whether they will have a way to contest that decision. That could be a concern when even long established digital artists like Loish have been falsely accused of using AI over on platforms like TikTok.

The update highlights the difficult balancing act of policing AI content. ArtStation has a big focus on concept art, and some in the industry now see generative AI as an inevitable part of the pipeline in this field. The new Disney deal with Adobe will focus on developing custom AI models specifically for concept work. In that context, KitBash probably sees banning AI art from the platform as counterproductive if not impossible.

#9142. Botticelli painting saved from leaving UK goes on view in Oxford

The Virgin and Child Enthroned being installed at the Ashmolean Museum

© Andrew Bailey, 2026, courtesy of the Ashmolean Museum, University of Oxford

A painting by Sandro Botticelli at risk of leaving the UK earlier this year has gone on display at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford where it was first shown in the 1930s.

The Virgin and Child Enthroned (1470s) was bought by the London-based private collection Klesch Collection, which announced plans in May to loan the painting to the Ashmolean for three years. The painting was previously exhibited at the museum in 1934–35 when it was attributed to Botticelli's workshop.

The UK government placed an export bar on the Botticelli painting, valued at £10.2m, in May 2025. The UK Department for Culture, Media and Sport said that the painting had a recommended price of £9,960,000 (plus VAT of £272,000, which can be reclaimed by an eligible institution). The work was sold at Sotheby’s London in late 2024 for £9.7m (with fees).

The painting underwent conservation over the summer to remove discoloured varnish and later retouching, revealing well-preserved details of the Virgin and Child and restoring the original cooler tones, says an Ashmolean statement. The painting is also unusual for its generous use of gold leaf, “although earlier Italian painters regularly applied gold to the backgrounds of their devotional works, it was less widely used by Botticelli's time”, add the statement.

The Botticelli painting was housed in the Convent of San Giuliano in Florence in the early 19th century, and was later transported to a small chapel attached to a group of farmhouses in a nearby village. It then passed into the family of Giovanni Magherini Graziani, who sold it in November 1903 to the Italian dealer, Elia Volpi. Harriet Sarah Jones Loyd (Lady Wantage) bought the work in May 1904 for £5,000. The Botticelli painting had been kept at Betterton House, near Wantage, Berkshire, since 1944.

Founders A. Gary and Dr. Anita Klesch started the Klesch Collection with the acquisition of a set of Four Seasons by Giuseppe Arcimboldo in 2014. The collection of 15th-to-17th-century European art, which also includes works by Caravaggio, Sofonisba Anguissola and Rubens, is regularly loaned to museums and institutions worldwide.

The Acer NITRO 20 N20-101 is now as cheap as a budget laptop.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The RAM crisis has caused a spike in the price of PCs, and that's made 2026 a difficult year for creatives and gamers alike. The good news is that you might not have to wait to Black Friday at the end of the month to find a decent discount. Right now, AO has the Acer NITRO 20 N20-101 Gaming PC reduced by £568 to £1,031 – the price of a budget laptop.

The entry-level specs won't interest professional video editors (see our guide to the best desktop PCs for video editors if you're in that category), but dedicated Nvidia graphics mean this budget setup is ready to handle lighter content creation as well as gaming, and it would mark a step up from a laptop with integrated graphics.

This is an entry-level gaming PC with a Intel Core 5 processor, Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 8GB graphics, 16GB RAM and a 512GB SSD. It would struggle with editing heavy effects on high-resolution footage in a program like DaVinci Resolve, but the dedicated graphics will have you covered for photo editing and lighter video editing.

Whether it's for gaming or content creation, there are two big advantages of a desktop PC over a laptop. Firstly, you tend to get more bang for your buck in the first place. As a rule, you tend to get more powerful internals, in the form of a superior CPU and GPU and more RAM, compared to what you would get in a laptop at the same price point (of course, some of this is outweighed by the fact that you also need to invest in a monitor and peripherals).

But the biggest advantage of a desktop PC is upgradability. If you find you outgrow the RTX 5060 too quickly, or processes are getting bottlenecked and you need more RAM, or more storage, you can buy the additional internals that you need as you need them and upgrade the configuration yourself, potentially multiple times.

#9138. The Cabinetmakers’ Autumn Exhibition features a rug-wrapped chair and a giant candle holder

The 2026 edition of the Danish furniture show has opened at Museum Ordrupgaard, with works by 36 designers on show alongside historic paintings and sculptures.

For this year’s edition of the Cabinetmakers’ Autumn Exhibition, or Snedkernes Efterårsudstilling, designers were invited to contribute works that explore the relationship between light and form.

The theme was chosen to reflect this year’s venue, the Snøhetta-designed galleries of Museum Ordrupgaard, which house important works of French and Danish art from the 19th and 20th centuries.

“In both impressionism and furniture design, light becomes a means of shaping an atmosphere and creating a sense of presence,” the exhibition overview stated.

“While the painters explored the impact of light on colours and atmosphere, designers examine the encounter between light and form, materials and surfaces, as use, function and aesthetic fuse into one, and even minor details and variations in light influence our perception of the furniture.”

The results include a 1.8-metre-high floor lamp that looks like a candle holder, by designers Karen Kjærgaard, Nanna Gram and Peter Skrzipczyk, and an elm wood chair wrapped in a patterned wool rug, by designers Karin Carlander and Christian Street.

Other eye-catching works include a cube made out of squashed ceramic vessels, by ceramicist duo Claydies, and a heavy bronze piece designed to look like a lightweight woven chair by designer Hans Sandgren Jakobsen.

The Cabinetmakers’ Autumn Exhibition has been an annual fixture since 1981, but its origins go back even further.

It began as a revival of the historic Cabinetmakers’ Guild Exhibition, which ran from 1927 to 1966 and debuted some of Denmark’s most iconic furniture designs, from Børge Mogensen’s Spanish Chair to Hans J Wegner‘s Round Chair.

Most of the works are contributed by members of the association, which is made up of over 80 designers, architects and manufacturers, although a handful of guests are invited to join each year.

One of this year’s most attention-grabbing works was contributed by guest exhibitor Matteo Fogale, a Uruguayan designer based in Copenhagen.

Fogale partnered with lighting brand Astep on a family of curvaceous ash wood lamps of different heights, topped by rotating discs that double as both lights and dimmer switches.

August Ostrow’s Soft Structure Lamp is another of the guest works. The American designer took cues from folded metal forms found in heating and ventilation machinery to create his copper and paper table light.

Timber craft is well represented in the show, with one particularly impressive piece by designer Andreas Lund and cabinetmaker Søren Risvang Snedkeri.

The pair collaborated on a table with an experimental frame of slender pine rods and 3D-printed joints.

Anna Søgaard designed a pair of cherry wood frames with opposing curves, while Claus Landry Bjerre crafted a pine wood cabinet incorporating 3D-milled replicas of 3D-scanned hazel branches.

Notable works in other materials include Carlo Volf’s wire-frame lamp, Zeyu Rong’s curvy translucent screen, and a light formed of four triangular glass tubes by Jonas Trampedach and Viola Heyn-Johnsen.

The Cabinetmakers’ Autumn Exhibition is on show at Museum Ordrupgaard in Charlottenlund from 23 October to 13 December 2026. See Dezeen Events Guide for more design events around the world.

#9137. Women finally start to get pride of place with central London sculptures

Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue (2026) is the 16th Fourth Plinth commission Photo: Jeff Spicer/PA Media Assignments

London bristles with sculptures of men. Only 4% of public monuments in the city are devoted to named women, according to the charity Art UK. It says something about the national psyche that there are twice as many animal statues in the city as there are sculptures devoted to specific women. But right now a pair of radical new works depicting and made by women—Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue in Trafalgar Square, and Nicole Eisenman’s Stack outside the Royal Academy of Arts (RA) on Piccadilly—are making their presence powerfully felt in two of the most male-dominated locations in the capital.

In Trafalgar Square, surrounded by depictions of monarchs and militia and across from Admiral Nelson atop his 51m-high column, Self’s Lady in Blue painted bronze cuts a distinctive dash on the empty plinth to the northwest of the square that, since 1999, has hosted a programme of contemporary sculpture commissions. Head held aloft with her vivid blue dress clinging to her ample curves, she strides forth in high heels, exuding purposeful confidence and optimism. As with all Fourth Plinth sculptures, this impressive female will be in situ for two years, before going to a permanent home in Fornebu in Norway.

“She’s not an idol to venerate or a historic figure to commemorate, she’s an everyday young metropolitan woman much like those who use the square every day,” Self declared at the work’s unveiling, adding: “Lady in Blue is not static, she’s in motion… and I hope she inspires all who see her to find the optimism to move forward in community with all those around them.” In this spirit, Self sees her sculpture as an attempt to redress both racial and gender imbalance in public art whether in her native US, the UK or Norway. “In most cities there’s an underrepresentation of sculptures that depict women, and especially women of colour, so I think that it is important to add more images and visual representation,” she said.

Meanwhile, a few streets away outside the RA, which in 258 years has shown only two living women in its main galleries, New York-based Eisenman has erected Stack, a towering work at over 8m tall. This totem of figures and objects made from an assortment of materials, including bronze, oak, brass, steel, nylon, acrylic resin and tin, is currently having a friendly face-off with Alfred Drury’s grandiose bronze sculpture of Joshua Reynolds, the RA’s first president, who brandishes his paintbrush and easel just outside the main entrance. In 2021 Eisenman got to the shortlist for Trafalgar Square’s Fourth Plinth and now with Stack, she has created her own column, impressive in its scale and magnitude, but also irreverently anti-monumental.

Nicole Eisenman's Stack (2022-24), installed in the courtyard of the Royal Academy

Photo: Damien Griffiths. © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy the artist and Hauser & Wirth

At its base hunches a craggy, androgynous figure shod in Birkenstocks and with a wooden barrel strapped to its back. A stand-in for the artist, perhaps, abject and emphatically earthbound, clutching not a paintbrush but an empty wine glass. On top of the barrel, rising out of a puddle of what looks like gooey melted cheese is a giant potato, over which lolls a rusty leonine cat modelled on Edie, Eisenman’s studio companion. Rather than a posturing war hero, Stack is topped off by the amiably smiling seated figure of the late artist Phyllida Barlow, rendered in gleaming sky-blue aluminium and jauntily balancing a vase of flowers on her head.

Barlow, who died unexpectedly in 2023, was a Royal Academician. Given where this work is situated, it is hard not to see Stack as a memorial to this much loved and greatly mourned artist. Eisenman is a huge admirer of Barlow, whose colossally ambitious but always defiantly anti-hubristic sculpture she first encountered when they were both in the Carnegie International in 2013. They subsequently became friends to the extent that an apparently amused Barlow went to Eisenman’s New York studio in 2022 to be 3D-printed for this work—“She was really good humoured about it,” Eisenman recalled in a recent talk at the Royal Institution. But while undoubtedly honouring Barlow, Stack is also more than a tribute to one person.

Eisenman is reluctant to offer specific interpretations but in her talk she revealed that the work was conceived with London in mind, declaring: “It’s amazing to me that it is at the RA. I hope it can stay in London.” She also stated that Stack emerged during the pandemic and forms a personal testament to when, as she put it, “life got pared down to the basics: food, wine, art, my cat”.

In strikingly different ways but with similar underlying intent, Stack and Lady in Blue offer alternative monuments to aspects of all our lives that rarely get acknowledged, and most notably the power of great women of all ages and from all origins. May we see more of their kind in all our cities.

Why the Adobe MAX 2026 opening keynote has me feeling cautiously hopeful.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Adobe MAX is in full swing, and after this morning's keynote, I'm left feeling pleasantly surprised. I initially arrived with slight apprehension, expecting to leave fatigued and underwhelmed by the grand kickoff, especially regarding Adobe's ever-divisive AI developments. Instead, I must confess, I'm cautiously hopeful.

It's no secret Adobe is going full send on AI, after a full fleet of AI partnerships and Firefly taking centre stage, blossoming into a full-fledged creative studio. It could all start to feel a little existential, but beaming under the stage lights, future Adobe CEO Anil Chakravarthy assures me, "Adobe will meet you where you are”. And I start to believe him.

AI has persisted as a divisive topic among creatives, but Adobe has shown a refreshing self-awareness around the tension. Emerging on stage, vice president Deepa Subramaniam wastes no time addressing that "things feel uncertain” in the wake of AI.

Assurances of “reliability” and “safety” are thrown around, honing in on Adobe's legacy as a brand shaped and "built by creatives that care about the craft”. She assures the sceptics among the crowd (myself included) that for Adobe, "Creativity isn’t a side project; it’s a way of life,” and to my surprise, the typically eye-roll-worthy sentiment soothes me. At its core, it seems Adobe hasn't forgotten about the creatives that shaped its brand.

Deepa raises some valid points. In an increasingly content-driven world, more is asked of us. The humble graphic designer is now expected to be a web designer, motion designer, and social media maverick all in one – something that Adobe's “rich learning ecosystem” can solve, according to Deepa. Creatives are trapped in a battle with waning time and resources, with demand for content ever increasing. If handled correctly, time-saving AI could offer the respite we need, but it raises a moral dilemma. Where do we stop?

#9135. Sydney's Powerhouse Parramatta revealed ahead of public opening tomorrow

Photography by Ben Hoskings, Cieran Murphy, Sean Fennessy, Romello Pereira

The Powerhouse Parramatta museum in Sydney by architecture studios Moreau Kusunoki and Genton, which is described as the largest cultural project in Australia since the Sydney Opera House, is set to open tomorrow.

Located on the banks of the Parramatta River in western Sydney, the distinctive Powerhouse Parramatta museum is wrapped by a lattice exoskeleton of steel that acts both as facade and structure.

It was designed to “pioneer a new museum model” that redefines contemporary museum practice and culture.

“We designed the new Powerhouse Parramatta with the mission of calling the museum paradigm into question and conceiving a platform with limitless potential that evolves over time and through its users,” said Moreau Kusunoki.

Paris-based architecture studio Moreau Kusunoki was lead designer for the project, while Australian architecture firm Genton was the local architect. The 30,000-square-metre museum is split into two blocky forms connected on the upper levels.

A system of three-layered steel lattice wraps the exterior of the building, referencing the iconic structure of Sydney Harbour Bridge while also connecting to the industrial heritage and manufacturing traditions of the site.

“Together with engineer Jun Sato, we developed the concept of ‘lattice’ for the structural exoskeleton – a system of intricate lattices that are wrapped around the spaces of the museum and support their dynamic programming, providing total interior freedom,” Moreau Kusunoki explained.

“Through the dissolution of the structure into a fine, efficient three-layered lattice, we conceived an envelope that transcends scale in order to exist simultaneously as both intimate and iconic, becoming the museum’s most recognisable design element.”

The lattice exoskeleton serves as the building’s facade as well as structure, which enables column-free interior exhibition spaces that support the museum’s diverse programming.

These include Exhibition Space 1, which is described as the largest column-free exhibition space in Australia. At 18 metres high and spanning over 2,000 square metres, it features a mechanical hoisting door in five sections, allowing it to open to the public riverside terrace.

Along with seven more traditional exhibition spaces, the institution contains 30 residential studios, numerous co-working spaces and other community-led learning facilities.

Beneath the lattice exoskeleton, much of the facade is fully glazed to filter natural light into the interiors. These interstitial spaces are informed by the Japanese concept of mâ – the interval between things, people, and time – shaping moments of pause that foster reflection and informal interaction.

“The concept of ‘in-between’, or mâ in Japanese, is central to the design approach in all our projects,” said Moreau Kusunoki. “We carved these spaces throughout the museum’s design as an indispensable factor of placemaking.”

“In contrast with the opaque nature of the presentation spaces, we modelled the mâ spaces as transparent and full of natural light, looking over the Parramatta River below and onto the horizon and country beyond,” it continued.

“The potential of the interstitial spaces gives way for life and meaning to evolve and to naturally appear in between the defined spaces, while events and interactions arise ‘through the cracks’, thereby organically enhancing the impact of the project.”

The two blocks, which were designed to open up on the ground floor, stand on two sides of a riverside terrace that sits above a garden that slopes down to the river. According to the museum, two-thirds of the site is dedicated to landscaped public space, with indigenous plant species planted under the guidance of the local First Nation community.

A rooftop terrace features a garden and a greenhouse, while an observatory with telescopes sits beneath a retractable roof. The museum’s ING Garden Pavilion will be used for hosting talks and workshops alongside community and industry programmes.

The neutral palette continues from the exterior to the interiors, with internal walls clad with glassfibre-reinforced concrete (GRC) panels of various textures.

They were made with quartz aggregate, waterglass-finish concrete and hand-applied oystershell render, adding tactile surfaces to the interior to create a calm exhibition viewing experience.

The building has been designed to operate at net-zero carbon.

Sustainability is embedded across the project, from renewable energy and water systems to zero-waste exhibition principles, making it the first public building in Australia to be assessed as a 6 Star Designed project under the Green Building Council of Australia‘s new Green Star Buildings assessment tool.

Five major international exhibitions will open tomorrow as part of the opening programmes of Powerhouse Parramatta, including Task Eternal, an immersive exhibition exploring humanity’s journey into space, which will be presented at Exhibition Space 1, and designed by Chinese architecture studio Open Architecture.

Dezeen is partnering with Powerhouse Parramatta to host two talks exploring the design and making of the landmark new museum. as part of the opening celebration.

The first brings together the architects, engineers and construction teams behind the building, while the second sees Dezeen co-CEO Benedict Hobson in conversation with OMA/AMO managing partner David Gianotten about The Mall – an ambitious exhibition examining the evolution of shopping centres and their influence on architecture, retail and contemporary culture.

A total of 179 events will take place across three weeks following the opening day as part of the opening festival programme, showcasing over 3,000 objects, including over 1,600 from Powerhouse Museum’s own collection.

Dezeen will also publish an exclusive video interview with architects Moreau Kusunoki and Genton, alongside four social videos exploring the museum’s inaugural exhibitions, including Task Eternal, The Mall and Es Devlin’s The Turning, showcasing the breadth of design, creativity and ideas behind the museum’s opening programme.

The creation of the new Powerhouse Parramatta museum, and the expanded research and public facilities at Powerhouse Castle Hill completed in 2024, form the $1.3 billion infrastructure renewal programme for the largest museum group in Australia. The renewal of the heritage Powerhouse Ultimo is still on going and expected to complete by late 2028.

Other recent landmark projects completed in Sydney include the Western Sydney International Airport, open to public last month, and Sydney Fish Market, which claims to be the largest fish market in the southern hemisphere.

Photography by Ben Hoskings, Cieran Murphy, Sean Fennessy, Romello Pereira

#9134. Soldier Designs Limited-Edition Hublot Timepieces in Latest Artist Collaboration

Swiss luxury watchmaker Hublot is expanding its roster of artist collaborations. Its latest partnership is with Soldier (born Leonard Iheagwam), a Nigerian-born, London-based visual artist, designer and skateboarder.

Soldier has created 50 timepieces for Hublot in black ceramic and black-plated titanium adorned with little toy sliders and a cross. They’re a recurring motif in the artist’s work, which he first debuted in 2024 with Angelica Mara Jopling of Incubator. The dial of the 42 mm chronograph features more toy soldiers inside the dial and bezel. The collaboration with Hublot has been two years in the making, with products starting at £22,900 ($30,303). Related Articles ARTnews, Art in America, and Hublot Host Dinner at New York Headquarters of KidSuper $160K Jean Arp Sculpture Stolen from Art Cologne Booth

“The collaboration came together really organically. I was invited to the Daniel Arsham collaboration preview in 2024 and at the time I had made a few paintings that needed a space to preview, Hublot let me do it in their London store, which led to them asking me to do create a London watch,” Soldier told ARTnews during a preview at the Hublot store on New Bond Street.

Soldier says the process of designing the timepiece was “the same” as painting, invoking Marcel Duchamp’s Fountain (1917), in the sense that that both objects are “ready-made.”

“A watch is already an object, which has thought behind it, and so the process is quite simple,” said Soldier. He first visited the brand’s Swiss headquarters to witness the watchmaking process. “Art and watches are not mass-produced items, there are actual engineers who work on creating such a piece,” he said, adding that he never wore a watch growing up. He now ears a Hublot, engraved with prhase, “artist proof.”

The toy soldiers in the watch and in Soldier’s artwork are a nod to the artist’s upbringing in Nigeria, and the cross symbolism links to his father, who is a reverend: “We didn’t really come from a lot of money, and growing up, I used to skateboard wearing camouflage clothing, so I had a lot of run-ins with the police and army because civilians weren’t allowed to wear camouflage because of the civil war.

He moved to England in 2019, and his work today draws deeply on his adolescence. His solo exhibition at Jopling, titled “When The Saints Go Marching,” featured paintings inspired by memories of the war, as well as more nostalgic scenes: religious iconography and portraits of his family.

Soldier teased that he’s working on a “big” show for 2028 without revealing the name of the institution. He called the secret upcoming show “very important” because within the Nigerian creative scene. From his perspective, there visual art hasn’t taken off to the same degree as the fashion industry, citing Lagos Fashion Week.

“I didn’t grow up thinking I could be a painter, neither could my parents. I’ve only been showing work for the past three years,” said Soldier, who now counts art world figures like Charlie Gosling, Lorenzo Amos and Robert Nava as friends.

The Caixa's first rebrand in almost 30 years builds on the existing foundations.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Banks don't always have the most exciting branding, but Brazil's Caixa Econômica Federal, a huge state-owned financial institution with 165 years of history, has a good go. The bank's rebranded for the first time in almost three decades, and the new identity ticks all the boxes.

The new identity is a fine example of a redesign done right. It feels more modern, more human and approachable, and it remains instantly recognisable, maintaining a clever hidden symbolism.

See our guides to the best laptops for graphic design and the best monitors for graphics artists if you need new tools for your own work.

The Caixa rebrand was the work of the Brazilian agency Tátil. It looked to the bank's history and its existing identity, kept the elements that people most recognised, and turned them up.

The previous logo design had lasted 29 years, so it was doing something right, but it was starting to look drab and dated with the old corporate feel of those muted colours and slightly italicised all-caps letters.

The rebrand turns the colours up with more modern, vibrant hues. Tátil suggests the blue represents enduring solidity while the orange reflects the diversity of Brazil.

The wordmark gets a cleaner lowercase design, and the core X motif, which features in the wordmark and also stands alone, gets a significant refresh.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The letter now more clearly resembles a box when applied in repeating patterns, reflecting the bank's name, which means box (as in savings box) in Portuguese. It also continues to resemble the roof of a house, reflecting the bank's role as Brazil's biggest mortgage lender.

You can see the evolution of the institution's branding in the video below.

"While every app was busy calling itself a bank, we went against the grain and found what only Caixa has, a bank that brings together the social and the commercial, today's needs and the drive to grow," Tátil says of the rebrand.

#9132. Aluminium canopy encases waterfront pavilion in Providence by Architecture Research Office

Steel columns support the expansive canopy of this green-roofed pavilion at 195 District Park in Providence, Rhode Island, which has been completed by New York-based studio Architecture Research Office.

Conceived by the studio as a “year-round amenity” for the public, the 195 District Park Pavilion accommodates two local businesses, an indoor-outdoor dining area and public restrooms overlooking the Providence River.

The pavilion’s position at the park’s highest point led Architecture Research Office (ARO) to design its multifaceted structure as a “beacon” that would be accessible from multiple entrances.

“Centrally located within 195 District Park, the pavilion is a park amenity that welcomes and orients visitors while supporting park programming,” studio principal Kim Yao told Dezeen.

“The pavilion is located at the highest point within the park in response to the floodplain of the adjacent Providence River.”

“This positioning created an opportunity for the building to serve as a beacon, visible from multiple entry points to the park,” Yao added.

Fronted by a plaza, the pavilion is composed of a metal frame that has been cloaked with cedar wood in a nod to the area’s local architecture.

Its structure is wrapped by an expansive aluminium canopy, which is supported by a series of steel columns and extends over the plaza to shelter an outdoor seating space.

Atop the structure, the sloped green roof helps to blend the pavilion into its surrounding landscape, while also limiting stormwater run-off and screening the rooftop’s mechanical systems.

“As a year-round amenity, the pavilion opens to shaded exterior areas in the summer while providing shelter during colder seasons,” Yao said.

“It also provides occupants with views of the river and surrounding areas,” she added.

Inside, the 3,500-square-foot building opens up to the indoor seating area, complete with exposed wooden joists.

Flanking the space are the pavilion’s operable storefront doors, which open up to the adjacent plaza and enable passive ventilation throughout the space.

Additional facilities include public restrooms located at the pavilion’s southern corner.

Its structure is perched beside a curved pedestrian bridge completed by Inform Studio and Buro Happold in 2020 that stretches over the Providence River to link two parks on the east and west sides of the city’s riverfront.

Other pavilions recently featured on Dezeen include a temporary marketing space in São Paulo built from mass-timber scrap and a basket-like aluminium pavilion in New York.

#9131. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review: A sublime remake that enhances and enchants in equal measure

Ocarina of Time is a stunning remake, but beneath its enchanting visuals and smoother controls enabled by modern technology, its core remains faithfully intact, reminding us why it still deserves to be regarded as one of the greatest games of all time.

Gorgeous, detailed and enchanting visuals

Original story and quests faithfully retained

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Since its 1998 release, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has been revered as the greatest game of all time, influencing many games, though few have ever tried to replicate its formula beyond subsequent 3D Zelda titles. That is, until Breath of the Wild blew open the doors, reinventing Nintendo's most beloved series in the modern open-world age of player agency and freedom, and its sequel, Tears of the Kingdom, reached new, unimaginable heights.

Returning to the N64 classic then might feel like a quaint relic of the past. So it's a revelation that, for the series' 40th anniversary, revisiting this beloved masterpiece remade for Nintendo Switch 2 has achieved an alchemy that rekindles the magic of what it must have been like to play Ocarina of Time for the first time 28 years ago.

This technically isn't the first time that Ocarina of Time has been remade, but whereas the 3DS update was largely a refurbishment that nonetheless stuck to the original blueprints, this Switch 2 remake has been fully rebuilt from the ground up for a new generation. The most notable difference, of course, is the art direction, which isn't just an exercise in Unreal hyper-realism. There's such attention to detail, from every blade of grass to the ridiculously detailed patterns and textures that adorn Link's hat and tunic. What's remarkable is that, unlike most modern games, all this visual density hasn't come at the expense of readability. I'd argue it's even easier to make out the cracked walls that bombs can blow up, while dungeons like the infamous Water Temple have improved architecture that makes navigation less confusing.

Despite initial divisive responses to the new Zelda character designs (but then, I'm old enough to remember the 'Celda' reactions to Wind Waker), I soon found myself enamoured by the ornate puppet-style aesthetic reminiscent of fairy-tale and fantasy media from the 80s, while the still-mute Link says a lot just with his subtle facial expressions. Admittedly, Sheik is much less androgynous than the original game (though the twist is about as non-spoiler as Luke Skywalker's father), but Zelda herself is also an improvement over the dainty damsel, with a voice distinct from the stereotypical princess in the newer games.

It's also however not a 'reimagining' in the vein of Resident Evil 2 where the original story has been adapted to a modern iteration of the series, nor is it just a primarily graphical overhaul like Metal Gear Solid Delta: Snake Eater that otherwise plays almost identically. After Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom's vast open world, trekking across Hyrule Field in a matter of minutes should feel ridiculously small, yet I have to give kudos to Nintendo for not succumbing to the temptation of stretching it out and then stuffing it with filler content, though the original side quests, from item-trading to hunting down Gold Skulltulas, are intact.

There's still a majesty to this finite adventure of a courageous boy journeying across time to save the world that still evokes so much, whether it's when you first pull out the iconic Master Sword or just stand in the middle of Hyrule Field and just make out the surrounding locations based on their distinct landmarks without the need for waypoint markers. A maximalist Final Fantasy 7 Remake approach that stretched the narrative with many more things to do would have diluted, rather than enhanced, the experience.

Still, plenty of modern additions make for a much smoother playthrough, from a free-moving camera to 60FPS performance in stark contrast to the original's barely stable 20FPS, and a clear quest log that also weaves a beautiful tapestry chronicling your adventure. There's even a dedicated jump button for Link, which admittedly took me a while to adjust to, since I kept falling off platforms when I expected an auto-jump; you can just dash instead of the original's hack of rolling around ad infinitum.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

You can also see some of the newer games' design incorporated, such as being able to quick-select items, though die-hards may lament that this means getting rid of the ability to map three items at once - it's balanced out by having some items like the lenses of truth or iron boots being mapped to respective buttons on the D-pad. Weapons like the slingshot, bow, and hookshot can also use gyro aiming, and while this was introduced in Ocarina of Time 3D, those still retained the original's first-person perspective, whereas now it's third-person like the newer titles, and you can move around at the same time.

Personally, my favourite new feature exclusive to Switch 2 hardware is being able to play the iconic ocarina songs by humming the tunes into the console's built-in microphone. For sure, it's a gimmick, but a very apt one, and I found it so much more intuitive than trying to memorise the button inputs, which is also a testament to how memorable Ocarina of Time's music continues to be.

If there is a downside to all the modern polish, it's that playing through Ocarina of Time is perhaps a little too breezy. That's certainly true of all the target and archery minigames, where, with the intuitive gyro aiming, I could get the top prizes on the first go without breaking a sweat. That also speaks to the absence of a more challenging option such as a Hero mode (you can opt to not increase your hearts, which is easier to do as you have to press a button to pick up heart containers), though an obvious choice would have been a Master Quest mode that remixes the dungeons, which could still happen post-launch either as a free update or paid DLC.

But Ocarina of Time was never as hardcore as Dark Souls; it was more about the pleasure of discovering new items you could put to ingenious use, especially against its brilliantly designed bosses, including an improved multi-stage finale. It's also nice that one of the remake's genuinely new features is a museum of all the enemies you've encountered, which lets you jump into boss rematches and even boss rushes.

If the overall changes to the game and story are relatively minor – voiced cutscenes are fine but hardly a gamechanger, though it's nice that Matt Mercer reprises his role as Ganondorf – it's really a testament that the original 1998 release was already such a defining moment in gaming that it doesn't require a radical overhaul to remind you just how great it still is. More importantly, in a post-BotW world, it's a relief that an adventure of this size can still feel epic and timeless.

Alan Wen is a freelance journalist writing about video games in the form of features, interview, previews, reviews and op-eds. Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

#9130. Tesla "winding down" production of Cybertruck

According to a recent tweet by Tesla founder Elon Musk, the electric vehicle company will be decreasing production of the Cybertruck at its Texas Gigafactory, just two and a half years after the car’s debut.

Musk said on Friday morning that Cybertruck production will be “winding down” to “make room” for the Cybercab, an electric sedan Tesla unveiled in 2024.

The change will go into effect starting mid-2027, according to Musk. It is unclear if the Cybertruck will be completely discontinued, although Musk agreed with a user of Musk-owned social media platform X, who called the news an “end of an era”.

“True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time”, the Tesla founder replied.

Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production

The Texas Gigafactory outside of Austin is the only factory known to produce the Cybertruck, according to MSN.

The shift may be due to poor sales of the vehicle since it was delivered to customers starting in late 2023.

The company sold 20, 237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024, representing a 48 per cent drop, according to an estimate from Kelley Blue Book.

Musk estimated the company would sell an average of between 250,000 and 500,000 trucks annually at a 2023 shareholders’ meeting.

The Cybertruck design was first unveiled in 2019. It quickly divided opinion for its boxy shape and sci-fi appearance.

It was launched and placed in showrooms in 2023. Shortly after, many models were recalled in 2024 due to faulty pedals.

Tesla has been shifting its factory lines in recent years, seemingly to usher in the production of its semi-autonomous products.

One example is the Cybercab due to be folded into the company’s robotaxi service.

Earlier this year, Tesla announced it shifted production lines for its Model S and Model X vehicles into fabrication of its Optimus humanoid robot, which recently went into production in California.

The company also debuted a flying Roadster concept car to much fanfare last month.

#9129. Newark Museum of Art restores ownership of David Drake jug to artists’ descendants

David Drake, Jug, 1852. Stoneware, 36.8cm by 27.9cm. Collection of The Newark Museum of Art. Ethically acquired from the Dave the Potter Legacy Trust LLC, established for the benefit of the artist’s descendants. The work was returned to the artist’s descendants by the Newark Museum of Art and subsequently purchased by the Museum from the Trust. Purchase 2026 Mr. and Mrs. William V. Griffin Fund and Barbara Harrison Wescott Fund. Photo by Richard Goodbody

This past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in New Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852. Just a few months later—lightning speed in museum time—The Art Newspaper has learned that the institution has reached an agreement with Drake’s heirs to restore ownership of the work and purchase it back for its permanent collection.

The arrangement comes just over a year after the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston reached an historic agreement with Drake’s family to return two major stoneware vessels, one of which the museum purchased back. Momentum built from there and return agreements were reached with institutions including the Telfair Museums in Savannah and the Georgia Museum of Art in Athens, Georgia, the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, and others.

“What happened this July was really special,” says George Fatheree, an adviser to the Drake family. A letter the Newark Museum sent to the artist’s descendants and shared with The Art Newspaper states: “We acquired a jug by your ancestor in 2022 to help us more powerfully teach the history of enslavement and enslaved labour, as part of the 2023 reimagining and reinstallation of our American art galleries, Seeing America: 18th and 19th Century.” Noting the MFA Boston partnership, the museum extended the opportunity to meet and “identify ways we might collaborate”.

According to Lisa Funderburke, the Newark Museum’s director and chief executive, it was the museum’s senior director of registration and collections management, Amber Germano, who first approached her over the summer and asked if she would be willing to sign a letter.

“It’s not uncommon for curators to visit my office with a stack of papers of things that are either for consideration or ongoing engagement on articles of repatriation,” Funderburke says. “Always my first question is: ‘Can you articulate to me what we’re doing here and what the impulse behind that is?’”

According to Yaba Baker, one of Drake’s fourth great-grandsons, Funderburke credited her staff with the initial action. “Lisa understood immediately what needed to be done,” Baker says. “One thing my family all agreed on: Dave is such a powerful figure in art history and Black history that to take the pots out of public view would be a disservice.”

Things moved quickly after that, with additional family meetings and Funderburke’s conversations with board members and other leaders at the museum. “I felt like this would be a strong north star for our board about where we are and where we want to be, and position ourselves as a museum into the future,” the director says.

After the museum commissioned several appraisals of the ceramic vessel, a value of around $135,000 was decided on. Numerous Drake pots have sold for five- and six-figure prices; the current record at auction for one of his works is the $1.65m paid for his 25-Gallon Poem Jar (1858), achieved at Crocker Farm Auctions in Maryland in 2021.

“Our approach is this should not be a zero-sum game,” Fatheree says, describing the outcome in Newark as a “win-win”.

Baker concurs, stressing the enduring lessons of Drake’s legacy. “He was a slave. He was considered three fifths of a person by the US constitution,” Baker says, adding that anti-literacy laws in South Carolina at the time forbade teaching enslaved people to write.

“For our family, it’s telling the story of someone who was considered by a lot of people to be nothing, but he conducted himself with such excellence,” Baker says, before quoting a famous inscription Drake wrote on another of his vessels that begins, “I wonder where is all my relation”, and concludes: “Friendship to all.”
